docs.title: OpenInterceptor
docs.text:
OpenInterceptor is an open-source, moddable space-combat simulator engine, written in Rust, for macOS and Linux first (Windows kept buildable).

Its reference content is X-COM: Interceptor (MicroProse, 1998), the fourth game in the X-COM series, after UFO Defense (Enemy Unknown), Terror from the Deep and Apocalypse. In the same way that OpenXcom and OpenApoc play their games, the engine reads the data from the player's own copy (installed or the CD) and plays it. No original content is in the repository, ever.

Goals, in priority order

  1. Modding first. The engine should make it easy to build a custom space simulator or campaign: new ships, weapons, stations, missions and a tech tree, written as data packs and scripts. The most likely use is a campaign that uses none of the original assets. Interceptor is the worked example that proves the engine is complete.
  2. Be an example of good Rust practice for a 3D application or game engine: clear layering, small dependencies, modules commented for a Rust beginner, and unit tests for all code. See Learn Rust with this codebase and Best practices.
  3. Play X-COM: Interceptor from the player's data on current systems.

The same order is in the repository's CLAUDE.md project rules.

Site version 0.25.0; Definition and Specification 1.19.0 (revision history).

docs.title: Where things are
docs.text: Branch / folder Holds main The engine: Cargo.toml, src/, the default campaign in resources/default/, bundled mods in packs/, the console page in web/console/, the gate scripts/check.sh docs (this site) Plan, architecture, original formats, modding guide, tests and status resources/xcom/, resources/xcom-cd/ (git-ignored) The developer's own original data: an installed copy (tried first) or a CD copy. Never committed dist/ (git-ignored) Local builds that may contain the player's data. Never shared

docs.title: Status
docs.text: Stage 0 (foundation and format analysis) is complete. Stage 1 (the flight simulator testbed) is complete, signed off on 2026-11-10 — every original ship, station and cockpit flies or renders from the player's original data, an original-free pack plays without it, any original asset can be replaced by a mod file (with --extract producing editable copies), and cockpits can be HD repaints or 3D models. Stage 2 (combat, objects and behaviours) is complete in app 0.3.0, which also carries Stage 3 part 1 (missions). App 0.3.1 delivers the playtest fixes of the Stage 3 interlude: a drift readout and flight-path marker, shot physics, visibility (rim light, distant dots, brightness), the killed mission result and a keys overlay (?). App 0.4.0 adds the first tablet control console (C1: pair a tablet on the local network, live telemetry, every action as a button — Tablet console); 0.4.1 fixes a start-up shader error; 0.4.2 moves the default campaign to resources/default, with the player's optional original data in resources/xcom (installed copy) or resources/xcom-cd (CD copy). See implementation status and the plan.

docs.title: How work flows: Rapid Prototyping
docs.text:
The project follows the Rapid Prototyping workflow (Workflows). Each user request becomes, in the same pass and before any code, a feature (F-…) on the Definition, then requirements (R-…) citing it on the Specification, then issues queued in sio citing those requirements. There are no approval gates; the definition and specification are a permanent record that moves ahead of the code. When the prototype is complete they seed the formal definition and specification of a production version, built through the SpecItOut fast track.

Definition and Specification 1.0.0 (2026-11-11): 79 features and 168 requirements, those for the code already built marked reverse-engineered; 1.1.0 marks the interlude's feedback items implemented; 1.2.0 adds the resources/ folder (F-CMP-005); 1.3.0 marks console C1 and the resources/ layout implemented and records protocol v1; 1.4.0 – 1.6.0 add the console heartbeat, collisions with impact and Simple physics; 1.7.0 plans the Mod Designer, Cutscene Designer and game bundling and records the console pairing fix and keep-awake (change history). Until sio supports a prototype kind the project runs as kind: implementation with spec pointing at docs/specification (DEV-042).

docs.title: Licence and repository
docs.text: The engine is MIT (LICENSE). The repository is public at github.com/bbogovich/OpenInterceptor; issues are GitHub Issues, reached through the sio client. X-COM and Interceptor are trademarks of their owners; this project is not affiliated with or endorsed by them.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The definition says what the player or modder gets from OpenInterceptor, and why. It is written in terms of features: a feature names an outcome ("a modder can replace any asset"), never the mechanism that delivers it. The specification turns each feature into testable requirements; the implementation builds them.

Definition version 1.19.0 (96 features). Changes are listed in the change history.

docs.title: Areas
docs.text: Area Code Features Covers Flight FLT 8 How a craft moves: the flight model, speed management, the arena, hyperspace and flight in an atmosphere over terrain. Combat CMB 11 Weapons, damage, ship systems, special equipment, targeting, wingmen and the enemies' behaviour. Cockpit & HUD HUD 9 What the pilot sees: cockpits, views, instruments and the targeting display. Controls & control console CON 9 How the pilot commands the craft: keyboard, mouse and gamepad bindings, finding the controls, and the tablet control console. Missions MSN 7 Battles with a purpose: roles, waves, objectives, outcomes, the debrief, environments and balance. Strategy & logistics STR 9 The real-time strategy game around the battles, and the default campaign's supply-chain logistics. Strategy interface UI 6 How the player works the strategy game: the original's separate full screens and dialogs, laid out by each campaign as data, with the single-grid testbed screen as an option. Campaigns CPN 7 The campaigns that ship with the engine, how one is chosen and played, and what turns battles into a story. Background on each campaign is in the pages beside this one. Modding toolkit MOD 15 What a modder gets: packs, readable rule files, asset replacement, translation, conditions, the tools that check and generate content and, planned, the Mod Designer (with 3D cockpit instrument placement), single-file models, the Cutscene Designer and cutscenes. Compatibility (original data) CMP 5 Playing X-COM: Interceptor from the player's own CD, read as data, without the project ever holding original content. Platforms PLT 5 Where OpenInterceptor runs and how it is shipped, including a creator's own bundled game. Testbed & tools TST 5 The testbed that every stage ends in, the viewers, headless runs and the asset generators.

docs.title: Reading a feature
docs.text:
Each feature is a heading F-<AREA>-NNN Title with:

  • What the player or modder gets, and Why;
  • Status: implemented, in-progress or planned;
  • Source: the user's request, quoted where known, or the plan item;
  • Specified by: the requirements that state it precisely.

Feature IDs are permanent: a feature that is dropped is marked so, never renumbered.

docs.title: Background
docs.text: The Campaigns pages describe the three campaigns that define "done" — the original Interceptor campaign, the original-free default campaign and Interceptor Remastered — and the game design that the mod formats implement.

docs.title: Cockpit & HUD
docs.text:
What the pilot sees: cockpits, views, instruments and the targeting display.

Requirements for these features: Cockpit & HUD requirements.

Feature Status F-HUD-001 Cockpits and views Implemented F-HUD-002 Mod cockpits: HD art and 3D models Implemented F-HUD-003 Flight instruments Implemented F-HUD-004 Targeting display Implemented F-HUD-005 Cockpit layout editor Implemented F-HUD-006 Drift display Implemented F-HUD-007 Seeing other craft Implemented F-HUD-008 Atmosphere instruments Implemented

docs.title: F-HUD-001 Cockpits and views
docs.text:
What. Each hull has its cockpit; the pilot switches between cockpit, chase and external views, including a manually orbited chase camera.

Why. The original's views, on modern wide screens.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.9; DEV-006.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-001, R-HUD-002

docs.title: F-HUD-002 Mod cockpits: HD art and 3D models
docs.text:
What. A modder can replace a cockpit with high-resolution art in its own design space, or with a 3D model whose instruments sit on the dashboard.

Why. Modding first: HD and 3D cockpits in the manner of XWVM.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.17, 2.18 and 2.21; DEV-033.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-003, R-HUD-004

docs.title: F-HUD-003 Flight instruments
docs.text:
What. Radars with shield rings, a ship status display (the craft from above with its shields in bands fore and aft, tinted by its hull), speed, energy, shield and hull gauges, power and system readouts, multi-function display pages and a message line.

Why. The pilot must always know the craft's state.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.9, 2.17, 2.20 and 6.6 (the ship status display, a user request after a playtest); DEV-037.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-005, R-HUD-006

docs.title: F-HUD-004 Targeting display
docs.text:
What. Brackets on the target, a lead marker, lock indication, an off-screen arrow and a nav-point marker.

Why. Gunnery and navigation in three dimensions.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.9.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-007

docs.title: F-HUD-005 Cockpit layout editor
docs.text:
What. In the cockpit view the pilot or modder can move and resize instruments, place them on a 3D cockpit, and save the result as an addon.

Why. Modding first: instruments placed by eye, saved as data.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.22 (user feedback).
  • Specified by: R-HUD-008

docs.title: F-HUD-006 Drift display
docs.text:
What. The speed indicator shows forward speed and the sideways and vertical drift, with a flight-path marker showing where the craft is actually going.

Why. User request: "Indicator displaying current speed should display both X and Y since the physics system allows sideways drift."

  • Status: implemented (app 0.3.1)
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.1.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-009

docs.title: F-HUD-007 Seeing other craft
docs.text:
What. Other fighters are easy to see at combat ranges, and the player can set the picture's brightness.

Why. User request: "it is difficult to see other fighters"; a brightness level.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.3.1)
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.3.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-010, R-HUD-011

docs.title: F-HUD-008 Atmosphere instruments
docs.text:
What. In an atmosphere the HUD shows altitude above the ground and vertical speed on the status line, and an artificial horizon with a pitch ladder.

Why. Needed to fly over terrain.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.6.0)
  • Source: Plan item 3.6.
  • Specified by: R-HUD-012

docs.title: F-HUD-009 Cockpits on wide screens
docs.text:
What. A cockpit drawn for 4:3 (the original's 640×480 art) looks right on a wide screen. A pack can define, per cockpit: - side bands that block the 3D view on either side of the cockpit art, in a colour (black by default), either full height or only beside the dashboard; - and/or extension art that fills those bands.

The view through the canopy keeps the same height whatever the screen's width.

Why. On a 16:9 or wider screen the 4:3 art sits in the middle, with space showing through at the sides, where the cockpit should be.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: User request, 2026-11-11: "we need to accommodate wide screens. The main problem is the cockpit consoles, which in the original proportions are 4x3 aspect ratio. Simplest solution is add override in the packs that extend the cockpit image to account for wider screens or to have a blackout area defined where the 3d view is blocked on either side of the cockpit base zone such that the player view vertical area remains consistent."
  • Specified by: R-HUD-013

docs.title: Combat
docs.text:
Weapons, damage, ship systems, special equipment, targeting, wingmen and the enemies' behaviour.

Requirements for these features: Combat requirements.

Feature Status F-CMB-001 Beam weapons Implemented F-CMB-002 Missiles and mines Implemented F-CMB-003 Damage and ship systems Implemented F-CMB-004 Power management Implemented F-CMB-005 Special equipment Implemented F-CMB-006 Targeting Implemented F-CMB-007 Wingmen and orders Implemented F-CMB-008 Enemies driven by data, with difficulty levels Implemented F-CMB-009 Stations with modules Implemented F-CMB-010 Damage looks, debris and explosions In progress F-CMB-011 Shot physics Implemented

docs.title: F-CMB-001 Beam weapons
docs.text:
What. Beam weapons draw energy, fire at their own rate and can be linked to fire singly, in pairs or all together.

Why. The original's gunnery model; energy makes power management matter.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.6.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-001, R-CMB-002

docs.title: F-CMB-002 Missiles and mines
docs.text:
What. Missiles need a lock and home in; special missiles sidestep, decoy, wait cloaked, split or copy a ship; mines blow up when an enemy comes near.

Why. Every weapon of both campaigns must fight as described.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.6 and 2.10.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-003, R-CMB-004, R-CMB-005

docs.title: F-CMB-003 Damage and ship systems
docs.text:
What. Hits strike the shield facing the attacker, then armour, then hull. Damage that gets through knocks out ship systems, which damage control repairs; a craft without engines and manoeuvring drifts disabled.

Why. The original's damage model; disabled ships can be captured.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.5.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-006, R-CMB-007

docs.title: F-CMB-004 Power management
docs.text:
What. The pilot shares a power budget between beams, shields and switched-on equipment, transfers energy and balances the shields fore and aft.

Why. A piloting function of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.6; DEV-024.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-008

docs.title: F-CMB-005 Special equipment
docs.text:
What. Tractor beam (tow and capture), cloak, ECM, point defence and sensor and jamming probes work in battle, for the player and for AI pilots.

Why. All are equipment of the original game; probes and point defence give both campaigns tactical depth.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.7 and 2.10.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-009, R-CMB-010, R-CMB-011, R-CMB-012, R-CMB-013

docs.title: F-CMB-006 Targeting
docs.text:
What. The pilot cycles targets, picks the nearest hostile or the one in the sights.

Why. A piloting function of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.7.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-014

docs.title: F-CMB-007 Wingmen and orders
docs.text:
What. Wingmen fly in formation and obey orders from a comms menu: attack my target, fire at will, evasive, retreat, status report.

Why. A piloting function of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.8 and 2.16; DEV-018 (resolved). User request, 2026-11-11: wingmen in formation "collide with the player and continue pushing … Formations probably need to have a bit more distance, and wingman fighters should actively try to avoid collisions."
  • Specified by: R-CMB-015, R-CMB-022

docs.title: F-CMB-008 Enemies driven by data, with difficulty levels
docs.text:
What. Every enemy type flies a behaviour written as data, with skill, fire discipline and use of its systems, and is harder or easier by difficulty level.

Why. Modding first: a modder writes new enemies without code. The original's AI is code, so its behaviours are derived.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.8 and 2.9; DEV-031, DEV-032.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-016, R-CMB-017

docs.title: F-CMB-009 Stations with modules
docs.text:
What. Stations carry turrets, shield generators and other modules at attachment points; destroying the hub takes the modules with it.

Why. Base assaults and defences of both campaigns.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.11.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-018

docs.title: F-CMB-010 Damage looks, debris and explosions
docs.text:
What. A craft looks more damaged as it is hurt, breaks into debris and explodes; stations can be shown under construction.

Why. Feedback on what the guns are doing; construction stages serve logistics.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan items 2.2–2.4 (XSPT sprite explosions and model-set extras deferred).
  • Specified by: R-CMB-019, R-CMB-020

docs.title: F-CMB-011 Shot physics
docs.text:
What. Shots leave the gun with the craft's own motion, so while the craft turns they still appear to fire forwards in a straight line relative to the pilot. Once fired, a shot is independent of where the craft points.

Why. User request: "Weapons, when fired, should start with the same angular momentum as the craft so that they appear to fire forwards in a straight line relative to the player." Decision D1 (2026-11-11): a rules option, physics by default.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.3.1)
  • Source: User request (feedback); decision D1; interlude item F.2.
  • Specified by: R-CMB-002, R-CMB-021

docs.title: Compatibility (original data)
docs.text:
Playing X-COM: Interceptor from the player's own CD, read as data, without the project ever holding original content.

Requirements for these features: Compatibility (original data) requirements.

Feature Status F-CMP-001 Play from the player's own CD Implemented F-CMP-002 Original formats read faithfully In progress F-CMP-003 No original content in the project Implemented F-CMP-004 Deviations on the record Implemented F-CMP-005 A resources folder that says what ships with the game Implemented

docs.title: F-CMP-001 Play from the player's own CD
docs.text:
What. The engine finds the player's copy of the CD data and plays X-COM: Interceptor from it.

Why. Compatibility objective; the project never holds original content.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.1, 1.13 and 1.14.
  • Specified by: R-CMP-001, R-CMP-002

docs.title: F-CMP-002 Original formats read faithfully
docs.text:
What. Original meshes, textures, images, sounds, rules and text are read as data and shown as the original intended; sprites and video follow.

Why. Compatibility objective.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan item 1.1; Stage 0 analysis; Smacker video and the MPSRC pack of talking heads read since app 0.12.0 – 0.13.1 (6.3, 6.6); XSPT outstanding (2.4).
  • Specified by: R-CPN-012, R-MOD-019, R-CMP-003, R-CMP-004, R-CMP-005, R-CMP-006, R-CMP-007, R-CMP-008, R-CMP-009, R-CMP-010, R-CMP-011

docs.title: F-CMP-003 No original content in the project
docs.text:
What. Nothing from the original game is committed or published in any form; original binaries are read as data, never executed.

Why. Legal and ethical: the player supplies the data.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Project rules.
  • Specified by: R-CMP-012, R-CON-021

docs.title: F-CMP-004 Deviations on the record
docs.text:
What. Where the engine differs from the original, or uses its own value where the original's is unknown, the difference is documented and facts are marked verified, derived or unknown.

Why. An undocumented deviation looks like a bug.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Project rules; Deviations page.
  • Specified by: R-CMP-013

docs.title: F-CMP-005 A resources folder that says what ships with the game
docs.text:
What. Content bundled with the game lives in one resources/ folder: - resources/default/ holds the default campaign and every one of its assets, in modern editable formats. It is the equivalent of the X-COM game's contents. - resources/xcom/ (an installed copy of X-COM: Interceptor) and resources/xcom-cd/ (a copy of the CD) are empty, git-ignored places where a player adds their own original data for a personal build.

Mods (packs/, and the user's mods folder) override resources as before. The interceptor campaign is such a mod.

Why. Most players will not own X-COM: Interceptor, and those who do more likely have it installed than a CD copy. A game/ folder at the root suggested the game itself was included. The new layout makes it explicit which assets the default campaign provides and what belongs to an installed mod.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.4.2, main bf7b7ce)
  • Source: User request, 2026-11-11: "Rather than a \"game\" folder in the repo root, which is misleading because it gives the impression that the game itself is there, it should be a \"resources\" folder that contains core assets bundled with the game for the default campaign in one subfolder, and gitignored xcom and xcom-cd subfolders that a user would manually add to for their personal build." "the default campaign's content in resources is the equivalent the xcom game contents, but with all files in modern editable formats."
  • Specified by: R-CMP-014, R-CMP-015

How the pilot commands the craft: keyboard, mouse and gamepad bindings, finding the controls, and the tablet control console.

Requirements for these features: Controls & control console requirements.

Feature Status F-CON-001 Rebindable keyboard, mouse and gamepad Implemented F-CON-002 Every original piloting function Implemented F-CON-003 One action catalogue, with a controls overlay Implemented F-CON-004 Tablet control console Implemented (except C5, the serial panel) F-CON-005 Console target viewport Implemented F-CON-006 Console 3D map Implemented F-CON-007 Physical control panel Planned F-CON-008 Console function-group tiles Implemented F-CON-009 Console themed by the active campaign Implemented

docs.title: F-CON-001 Rebindable keyboard, mouse and gamepad
docs.text:
What. Every action can be bound to two keys and two gamepad buttons or chords, with device settings, from a controls menu in the launcher and the pause menu.

Why. Players and their hardware differ; a gamepad has far fewer buttons than the keyboard.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.10 and 2.15; DEV-003, DEV-004, DEV-028. User request, 2026-11-11: "When mission is started by pressing enter on the menu or restart prompt, a laser fires immediately at start of mission because of the enter press. that first keypress should be suppressed." (R-CON-025, app 0.4.10).
  • Specified by: R-CON-001, R-CON-003, R-CON-004, R-CON-005, R-CON-006, R-CON-025

docs.title: F-CON-002 Every original piloting function
docs.text:
What. All piloting functions of the original game have a default key: power, tractor, cloak, ECM, hyperspace, wingman comms, message repeat.

Why. Compatibility: the original's keyboard layout and functions.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.16; DEV-001, DEV-027.
  • Specified by: R-CON-002

docs.title: F-CON-003 One action catalogue, with a controls overlay
docs.text:
What. A single catalogue of actions drives the key bindings, an in-flight overlay listing them, and the control console.

Why. User request: "There are a large number of keyboard shortcuts to keep track of."

  • Status: implemented (app 0.3.1): the keys overlay on ? or Shift+F1; since C1 (app 0.4.0) the console's catalogue is built from the same table.
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.5.
  • Specified by: R-CON-001, R-CON-007, R-CON-008, R-CON-011

docs.title: F-CON-004 Tablet control console
docs.text:
What. A web page served by the game turns a tablet on the local network into a second control surface beside a joystick or gamepad: live craft state goes out, the pilot's actions come back, in real time. The top row shows the exterior-view HUD; the centre a widened display console like the cockpit's; shield rings and shield controls sit on the left, power sliders on the right, and other functions grouped below. Off by default, local network only, paired with a code.

Why. Immersion, always knowing the craft's condition, and reaching features that are otherwise forgotten. Primary use: an iPad alongside a joystick or gamepad.

  • Status: implemented, except the physical panel (C5, F-CON-007). Console items C1 – C4 and C2b are done: C2 (app 0.4.11) the two layouts, All-in-one and Cockpit, with the function-group tiles and power sliders; C3 (0.4.14) the target viewport; C4 (0.4.15) the 3D map, radar contacts, tap to target and the message log; C2b (0.5.0) campaign themes. Verified in Chrome; an iPad pass is still to be run (MT-3-29 – MT-3-32). History: C1 (app 0.4.0) is built: the game serves the console page and a WebSocket (--console or console.enabled; port 8765, console.port), local network only, paired with a 6-digit code; the page shows live telemetry, a throttle slider and every action as a button, with features the craft lacks shown disabled. Since app 0.4.7 a tablet pairs from any screen, the launcher included, as soon as the sixth digit is typed; since 0.4.8 the page keeps the tablet's screen awake; since 0.4.9 buttons show clearly when pressed and the console shows brief static when the player's craft is hit. The layout described above came with C2 (app 0.4.11) as the Cockpit layout; the page offers it beside the C1 All-in-one layout, switchable on the page and remembered per tablet (user request, 2026-11-11: "ipad UI is very different from the design proposal but useful. the page should support two modes, the collected "all-in-one" control scheme in the current design, and the version from the proposal PDF."). See Tablet console.
  • Source: User request; decision D2 (off by default; local network only; pairing code; port 8765, changeable); interlude items C1 and C2. User request, 2026-11-11: "tablet goes to sleep while page displayed; some function in page needs to keep alive. browser will keep tablet alive during media streaming for video display, so there are some kind of mechanisms in place to prevent sleep. Unclear to what extent this is possible." User request, 2026-11-11: "Initial test on console works well, better button press feedback needed so that it's clean when user has pressed the button. for the style currently applied, the button should highlight with the border color and text switch to black. Add brief static effects when a craft is hit by weapons fire."
  • Specified by: R-CON-007, R-CON-009, R-CON-010, R-CON-011, R-CON-012, R-CON-013, R-CON-014, R-CON-022, R-CON-023, R-CON-024, R-CON-026

docs.title: F-CON-005 Console target viewport
docs.text:
What. The console's centre display shows the current target's model, turned to its true angle relative to the player.

Why. Knowing at a glance which way the target is facing.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.4.14, main e51eca9): the display console's Target tab draws the target's model in WebGL, flat-shaded and turned to its orientation relative to the player.
  • Source: User request; interlude item C3.
  • Specified by: R-CON-015

docs.title: F-CON-006 Console 3D map
docs.text:
What. The console's centre display toggles to a 3D map of the battle, modelled on TIE Fighter's map view.

Why. Situational awareness without leaving the cockpit view.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.4.15, main e2b5012): the Map tab shows every radar contact around the player, with range rings, height stalks, relation colours and three views; tapping a contact targets it.
  • Source: User request; interlude item C4.
  • Specified by: R-CON-016

docs.title: F-CON-007 Physical control panel
docs.text:
What. Longer term, a physical panel with lights and buttons (an Arduino over USB) works as a control console.

Why. Immersion for players who build their own cockpit.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: User request (longer term); interlude item C5.
  • Specified by: R-CON-010, R-CON-017

docs.title: F-CON-008 Console function-group tiles
docs.text:
What. The console's functions are grouped by ship system. Each group is a tile showing that system's status; tapping a tile opens a full-width strip with that group's controls and collapses the other tiles to their headers; tapping the open group's title closes the strip so every status card shows again; tapping another group's title switches the strip to that group. Every function group is shown for every craft; individual controls the current craft lacks (for example cloak or ECM not fitted, or no missiles) appear disabled and labelled as not fitted, and the status card shows those features as not fitted.

Why. User request (iPad UI): "since multiple options exist per function group, we will add a feature to make them easy to manage. The tiles present in the mockup will be used and show the status per system in the card. Tapping the tile will collapse other tiles to just their header, and present a full width strip with controls for that function group. Tapping title of the current view again collapses it so that the status cards are all visible. Tapping title of another function group switches the control display to that function group." User request: "Function groups not available at all for the current craft are not displayed. Available function groups are grouped at the horizontal screen center, with empty non-selectable groups where the remaining function group cards would usually be presented in same framing format but with no content." Superseded by the user: "actually based on design all are common, just with individual features disabled, so hiding the whole content is not necessary".

  • Status: implemented (app 0.4.11, main db2f264), in the Cockpit layout.
  • Source: User request (iPad UI); interlude item C2.
  • Specified by: R-CON-018, R-CON-026, R-CON-019

docs.title: F-CON-009 Console themed by the active campaign
docs.text:
What. The console's look comes from the active campaign or mod. For Interceptor the console uses new assets made for this project, kept in the interceptor pack, styled after the current craft's cockpit overlay, with every control clearly labelled. The default campaign uses its retro (art-deco) style. No original art is reproduced in the console.

Why. User request: "The visual style of the tablet interface is derived from the active campaign/mod. In the case of X-Com Interceptor, these are new assets in the default mod, and the visual styling is based on the current craft's cockpit overlay, but with everything clearly labelled. The default campaign, likewise, follows the retro aesthetic." Clarified by the user: "xcom console theme goes in the interceptor pack, default assets go in resources/default since it's the core content."

  • Status: implemented (app 0.5.0, main 0a1c340): a pack's rules set the console's colours, font and corners, per cockpit if wanted. The default campaign is art-deco (brass on midnight, Futura); interceptor keeps the green instrument look, tinted per cockpit (A olive bronze, B steel blue, C red). Colours only: no original art is used. See Console themes.
  • Source: User request (iPad UI); interlude items C2 and C2b.
  • Specified by: R-CON-020, R-CON-021

docs.title: Flight
docs.text:
How a craft moves: the flight model, speed management, the arena, hyperspace and, later, flight in an atmosphere.

Requirements for these features: Flight requirements.

Feature Status F-FLT-001 Newtonian flight, with an assisted option Implemented F-FLT-002 Flight computer: match and hold speed Implemented F-FLT-003 Afterburner and sideways thrust Implemented F-FLT-004 Arena boundary Implemented F-FLT-005 Hyperspace departure Implemented F-FLT-006 Collisions Implemented F-FLT-007 Atmospheric flight over terrain In progress

docs.title: F-FLT-001 Newtonian flight, with an assisted option
docs.text:
What. Every craft flies by thrust and momentum: it coasts when the throttle is off, slides through hard turns, slows with reverse thrust or a brake and is capped at its top speed. A campaign or mod may choose an arcade-style assisted model instead.

Why. A space simulator should feel like space; the arcade model of the first build slowed ships without thrust. Mods aiming at a different feel keep the choice.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; the owner's playtest of build 0.2.0 ("the arcade flight model slowed ships without thrust", Stage 1 plan).
  • Specified by: R-FLT-001, R-FLT-002, R-FLT-003, R-FLT-010

docs.title: F-FLT-002 Flight computer: match and hold speed
docs.text:
What. The pilot can match a target's speed and have the craft hold a forward speed while cancelling sideways drift. AI pilots fly with the same computer and the same limits.

Why. Newtonian flight is hard to manage in a dogfight without help; AI pilots must obey the player's physics to be fair.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; DEV-020.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-004

docs.title: F-FLT-003 Afterburner and sideways thrust
docs.text:
What. An afterburner raises top speed at an energy cost; craft with vectored thrust (VCT) can slide sideways and vertically.

Why. Both are piloting functions of the original game.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; original controls.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-005, R-FLT-006

docs.title: F-FLT-004 Arena boundary
docs.text:
What. A battle has an edge; a craft that reaches it is stopped there and told so.

Why. Under newtonian flight a coasting ship would otherwise drift away for ever.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.5; DEV-021.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-007

docs.title: F-FLT-005 Hyperspace departure
docs.text:
What. The pilot can jump out of a battle after a countdown, abort it, and take a craft held by the tractor along as a prize. Jumping out ends the battle as a retreat.

Why. Retreat and capture are part of the original game's battles.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.7, 2.16 and 3.8.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-008

docs.title: F-FLT-006 Collisions
docs.text:
What. Craft bounce off each other and off station hulls, and a hard hit has real consequences. The impact changes direction according to the relative speed, and the angle of impact sets the craft spinning, out of control for a moment. Ships pressed together make one impact sound, not a hammering series. Fast shots never pass through a target.

Why. Stations are large solid objects, and hits must count. A collision should feel like one.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 1.7; user request, 2026-11-11: "Formation flying - problems frequently occur where a wingman collides with the player and continues pushing, resulting in a \"hammering\" series of sounds. Formations probably need to have a bit more distance, and wingman fighters should actively try to avoid collisions. Collision should also cause more of an impact and result in directional changes and spin based on relative velocity and angle of impact. This will result in a collision causing fighter to \"spin out of control\". A collision that persists (fighter effectively pushing and staying attached to another) should only play the impact sound effect on initial impact."
  • Specified by: R-FLT-009

docs.title: F-FLT-008 Simple physics for beginners
docs.text:
What. A player-selectable physics mode, Simple or Realistic. - In Simple mode the player's craft always travels where its nose points, at a speed set by the engine power, with no drift: it flies like a traditional space fighter game. - Realistic is the Newtonian model with drift. - The choice is offered only on the campaign's first three difficulty levels. Higher levels always use Realistic.

Why. Beginners used to traditional fighter games find drift hard. Higher levels keep the full simulation.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: User request, 2026-11-11: "Add a physics mode toggle - Simple and Realistic. Simple physics will function more like a general space fighter simulator similar to x-wing, where navigation always follows the player direction based on direction and engine power without the physics drift applied. This makes it easier for beginner players who are used to more traditional fighter games. The toggle is only available on the first three difficulty levels, anything higher always uses realistic physics."
  • Specified by: R-FLT-013

docs.title: F-FLT-007 Atmospheric flight over terrain
docs.text:
What. On planet surfaces craft feel drag, gravity and lift, can hover and land, and fly over terrain with ground installations, a sky and fog.

Why. New to this engine: it lets campaigns fight on worlds, not only in space (the default campaign has surface missions).

  • Status: in-progress — drag, gravity, lift, hover, landing, crashing and the ceiling exit, generated and heightmap terrain, the sky and fog, and ground installations are built (app 0.6.0 – 0.6.1). Scattered objects and detail textures on the terrain remain (plan item 3.5).
  • Source: Plan items 3.3–3.5.
  • Specified by: R-FLT-011, R-FLT-012

docs.title: Strategy interface
docs.text:
How the player works the strategy game: the original's style of separate full screens and dialogs — the star map, bases, purchase, pilots, briefings and the rest — each laid out by the campaign as data, with the single-grid testbed screen kept as an option.

Requirements for these features: Strategy interface requirements.

Feature Status F-UI-001 Original-style strategy screens Planned F-UI-002 Screens and widgets as mod data Planned F-UI-003 Keyboard and gamepad on every screen Planned F-UI-004 The testbed layout as an option Planned F-UI-005 The default campaign's own screens Planned F-UI-006 Crisp and readable at any window size Planned

docs.title: F-UI-001 Original-style strategy screens
docs.text:
What. Playing Interceptor, the strategy game looks and works like the original: the CSD star map as the hub, with separate full screens for bases, purchase, manufacture, pilots, research, the hangar, reports, the UFOpedia, briefings and debriefings, and dialogs over the map for orders, launching a mission and alien transmissions — at the original's positions, with the original's art read from the player's own copy.

Why. Compatibility: the original "broke up functionality across multiple screens as opposed to a single grid".

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-12: "Critically missing from the game and requirements is the strategy UI from Interceptor. The gridded layout currently present is fine for testing, but we need to support the interface style the original game has. It broke up functionality across multiple screens as opposed to a single grid like currently present." — "there are additional screens, these are just a subset." Plan item 6.9.
  • Specified by: R-UI-001, R-UI-003, R-UI-004, R-UI-010, R-UI-011, R-UI-013, R-UI-019 – R-UI-021, R-UI-023 – R-UI-038, R-UI-040

docs.title: F-UI-002 Screens and widgets as mod data
docs.text:
What. A modder builds a campaign's interface from engine widgets — buttons, toggles, values, lists, maps, 3D views, text, portraits — placed by rectangle on full screens and dialogs that link to one another, binds them to the engine's screen functions and the campaign's own values, and can add screens of their own.

Why. Modding first: a custom campaign with no original assets gets an interface of its own design without touching code.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The same request; the existing Screens design (Format: interface); plan items 6.1 and 6.9.
  • Specified by: R-UI-001 – R-UI-013, R-UI-017, R-UI-019, R-UI-039, R-UI-040

docs.title: F-UI-003 Keyboard and gamepad on every screen
docs.text:
What. Every screen and dialog can be worked with the keyboard alone or a gamepad alone: a visible focus moves between the controls, and the keys can be rebound.

Why. The flight game is played with a gamepad; the strategy game should not force a change to the mouse.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: Plan item 6.9; the controls' one action table (F-CON-001).
  • Specified by: R-UI-014

docs.title: F-UI-004 The testbed layout as an option
docs.text:
What. The single-grid strategy screen of app 0.16 stays: a player can switch to it in the options, and a campaign without screens of its own uses it.

Why. The user: "The gridded layout currently present is fine for testing".

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-12; plan item 6.9.14.
  • Specified by: R-UI-018, R-UI-037

docs.title: F-UI-005 The default campaign's own screens
docs.text:
What. Perils of the Void has its own multi-screen interface in its art-deco style, with art generated by the project's tools, playable with no original data.

Why. Modding first: every feature works in the original-free campaign, which is the modders' worked example.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: Plan item 6.9.13; the project rules.
  • Specified by: R-UI-022

docs.title: F-UI-006 Crisp and readable at any window size
docs.text:
What. The original's 640 × 480 screens fill any window without distortion or blur, and every string can be translated without spilling out of its place.

Why. Played on today's wide, high-resolution displays, in any language.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: Plan item 6.9.1.
  • Specified by: R-UI-015, R-UI-016

docs.text: Version Date Change 1.19.0 2026-11-12 New area (user request): F-UI-001 – F-UI-006, the original-style multi-screen strategy interface; all planned

docs.title: Missions
docs.text:
Battles with a purpose: roles, waves, objectives, outcomes, the debrief, environments and balance.

Requirements for these features: Missions requirements.

Feature Status F-MSN-001 Missions as data Implemented F-MSN-002 Debrief Implemented F-MSN-003 Radio chatter and voices Implemented F-MSN-004 Environments and hazards Implemented F-MSN-005 Simulator missions Implemented F-MSN-006 Base defence the player can win Implemented F-MSN-007 Logistics missions In progress

docs.title: F-MSN-001 Missions as data
docs.text:
What. A mission is a data file: the forces taking part, when and where they arrive, waves, objectives, a timer, outcomes and chatter.

Why. Modding first: new missions without code.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 3.1 and 3.2; DEV-040.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-001, R-MSN-002, R-MSN-003, R-MSN-004

docs.title: F-MSN-002 Debrief
docs.text:
What. After a mission the player sees the result, kills, losses, time and optional objectives, and can retry. Jumping out counts as a retreat.

Why. Closure and feedback for each battle.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 3.8.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-005

docs.title: F-MSN-003 Radio chatter and voices
docs.text:
What. Pilots talk on the radio when things happen, in their own voices: wingmen answer orders and report losses, chatter lines can be spoken, and a computer voice announces the end of a mission.

Why. Atmosphere and information.

  • Status: implemented — chatter in app 0.3.0, voices in app 0.6.2. The interceptor campaign's numbered pilot clips are not mapped yet (which line each says is unknown; Open note on R-MSN-007); its computer voice is.
  • Source: Plan item 3.7.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-006, R-MSN-007

docs.title: F-MSN-004 Environments and hazards
docs.text:
What. Battles happen in open space, in orbit over a planet, in small pockets and above planet surfaces with ground installations, with hazards such as asteroid fields, black-hole pull, minefields and ion storms. Environments and hazards are pack data that a mission or scenario names.

Why. Variety, and the surface missions of the default campaign.

  • Status: implemented — hazards in app 0.5.1, environments in 0.6.0, ground installations in 0.6.1. Choosing the environment from the strategy map's location comes with Stage 4.
  • Source: Plan items 3.2 (hazards), 3.3–3.5.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-008, R-MSN-009

docs.title: F-MSN-005 Simulator missions
docs.text:
What. The player sets up and flies practice battles from a setup screen: any mission, in any environment, with hazards added and the enemy force scaled.

Why. The original has simulator missions; practice; trying a mission in other conditions without editing it.

  • Status: implemented (app 0.6.3): the launcher's Simulator. The interceptor campaign's own simulator mission types are part of its mission set (plan item 3.11).
  • Source: Plan item 3.9.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-010

docs.title: F-MSN-006 Base defence the player can win
docs.text:
What. In a base defence the player has time to engage more than one attacker before the base can fall, on every difficulty.

Why. User request: "Base destroyed too easily, player doesn't have time to engage more than one fighter before the aliens successfully destroy the base even on beginner."

  • Status: implemented (app 0.3.1). Measured, the base was not falling too fast: on the harder levels the player's craft was destroyed and the debrief showed the base-lost text. The player's death is now its own result, killed.
  • Source: User request (feedback); interlude item F.4.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-003, R-MSN-005, R-MSN-011

docs.title: F-MSN-007 Logistics missions
docs.text:
What. Convoy-ambush and construction-defence missions put the supply chain into battles.

Why. Gives escort and raid missions a strategic cause.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan item 3.13 (flown from the launcher; generation from the strategy layer is Stage 4). The convoy ambush is generated and flown from the strategy map since app 0.9.2, redesigned to the user's design (cargo pods, tugs, escorts); construction defence is not generated yet.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-012, R-STR-019

docs.title: Modding toolkit
docs.text:
What a modder gets: packs, readable rule files, asset replacement, translation, conditions, the tools that check and generate content and, planned, the Mod Designer and Cutscene Designer (design).

Requirements for these features: Modding toolkit requirements.

Feature Status F-MOD-001 Packs and mod kinds Implemented F-MOD-002 Readable rule files that explain mistakes Implemented F-MOD-003 Replace any asset, in open formats Implemented F-MOD-004 Text and translation Implemented F-MOD-005 Conditions, actions and scripting In progress F-MOD-006 Mod validation In progress F-MOD-007 Generated assets (recipes) Planned F-MOD-008 Modding guide In progress F-MOD-009 Mod Designer Planned F-MOD-010 Cutscene Designer Planned F-MOD-011 Cutscenes in the game Planned F-MOD-012 Video cutscenes Planned F-MOD-013 Shared formations In progress F-MOD-014 3D cockpit instrument placement Planned F-MOD-015 Single-file models and Blender sources Planned

docs.title: F-MOD-001 Packs and mod kinds
docs.text:
What. Content comes in packs: campaigns, addons that change a campaign, and libraries shared between them; a campaign can extend another.

Packs and mods. Both use the same format; the difference is where they come from and whether a build includes them:

  • packs are "baked into" the game on build: resources/ and the bundled packs/, included in a product bundle (R-PLT-007, R-PLT-008);
  • mods are added externally, in the user's local mods folder.

A mod that builds on another pack is an extension: the other pack is its base, and it adds to or overrides that pack's assets (R-MOD-023).

Open

Where exactly the line between a pack and a mod falls is to be settled: for example, whether a mod promoted into a product bundle becomes a pack. The user, 2026-11-11: "Will have to consider where the distinction is between pack and mod in that case, but conceptually packs are \"baked into\" the game on build where mods are added externally in user's local files."

Why. Modding first.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.1. Packs versus mods and the name extension: the user, 2026-11-11 ("Let's call it an extension as opposed to an override, since another pack is the base and we are either adding to or overriding assets.").
  • Specified by: R-CPN-001, R-MOD-001, R-MOD-002, R-MOD-003, R-MOD-004, R-MOD-011, R-MOD-019, R-CON-020

docs.title: F-MOD-002 Readable rule files that explain mistakes
docs.text:
What. Every mod file is plain YAML with units; mistakes are reported with file, line and key path and a suggestion; editors get JSON Schemas.

Why. A modder should never have to guess what went wrong.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.19 (user feedback); DEV-030.
  • Specified by: R-MSN-004, R-MOD-005, R-MOD-006, R-MOD-007, R-CMP-011

docs.title: F-MOD-003 Replace any asset, in open formats
docs.text:
What. Any original model, texture, image or sound can be replaced by a file in an open format (OBJ, PNG, TGA, WAV), and the originals can be extracted as editable copies.

Why. Modding first: HD and 3D replacements without redistributing original files.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 1.15 and 1.16; DEV-022.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-008, R-MOD-009, R-MOD-010

docs.title: F-MOD-004 Text and translation
docs.text:
What. All text is referenced by key and can be translated by an addon.

Why. Translations and new campaigns without editing code.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan item 2.1.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-012

docs.title: F-MOD-005 Conditions, actions and scripting
docs.text:
What. Behaviours, missions and campaign rules use a small checked language of conditions and actions; a second-tier script language is to be decided (evaluation recorded in 1.12.0, awaiting the user's decision).

Why. Rules that depend on the situation, without code changes.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan items 2.9, 3.1 and 3.10.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-013, R-MOD-014, R-MOD-015

docs.title: F-MOD-006 Mod validation
docs.text:
What. A modder can check a campaign and its addons headlessly and get every error at once.

Why. Mistakes found before playing.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan items 1.13 and 7.1.
  • Specified by: R-CPN-003, R-MOD-016, R-MOD-017

docs.title: F-MOD-007 Generated assets (recipes)
docs.text:
What. Mods can generate assets from the player's data (upscaled textures, patched meshes, recolours) reproducibly on the player's machine.

Why. Remastered content without redistributing original files.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: Plan items 7.2–7.6.
  • Specified by: R-CPN-006, R-MOD-018

docs.title: F-MOD-008 Modding guide
docs.text:
What. Documentation of every key, and tutorials from changing one number to building a new campaign.

Why. Modding first.

  • Status: in-progress
  • Source: Plan item 7.9; project rule: every new key is documented in the same change.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-020

docs.title: F-MOD-009 Mod Designer
docs.text:
What. A companion application, separate from the game, for building packs and mods without editing files by hand: - a new pack or mod — a campaign, an addon or an extension of another pack, which adds to or overrides its assets — starts from a chosen base (the default campaign, interceptor or any installed pack); - any asset of the parent can be imported: it is copied with its dependencies (a model with its textures, a ship with its model set, debris, sounds and text) and converted from original formats where needed; - the copy is edited in an external program such as Blender and reloads live; - forms generated from the engine's schemas, a raw YAML view, "where is this used?", validation on every save, play in the testbed, and packaging as a folder or zip.

Everything it saves is the same open pack data a modder could write by hand.

Why. Modding first: building a mod should not need a text editor and the file reference open side by side.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-11, quoted in full on the design page: "Add to the longer term plan a companion app for a mod designer, which allows a user to define custom packs and mods to add to the game. On creation of a new pack or mod, user may choose a base to use for assets that they are going to override. When editing a mod, they can choose to import an asset from the parent. This duplicates the original asset and its dependencies (model plus textures in most cases) which the user can then edit in an external program, usually blender." Decisions D1 (macroquad UI, no new dependency) and D5 (a separate program in the same repository; two build artifacts), 2026-11-11. The kind extension rather than override: the user, 2026-11-11. Plan items MD4, MD5.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-021, R-MOD-022, R-MOD-023, R-MOD-024, R-MOD-025, R-MOD-026, R-MOD-027, R-MOD-028, R-MOD-029, R-MOD-030

docs.title: F-MOD-010 Cutscene Designer
docs.text:
What. Inside the Mod Designer, a timeline editor for introduction films and story scenes played by the engine itself: - scripted entities, added and removed at set times, keyframed for position, rotation and speed (the speed is overridden when positions are keyed, so every key is met exactly), with timed actions: fire beams or missiles, chase, capture with the tractor, be destroyed, jump out; - autopilot entities flown by the beginner AI rules towards designated targets, as background action, with an optional aggressive flag; - a harmless flag that makes an entity's or an action's weapons fire without dealing damage; - groups placed by a chosen formation; - sounds at timed positions (narration, music, effects) and translatable captions; - cameras, fixed or attached to an object with keyframed distance and orbit, and camera cuts set by keyframes; - a 3D map of the whole scene and a preview of the current frame, with exact seeking from snapshots; - deterministic playback with Simple physics.

Why. Campaigns need films for their story; a modder should be able to make them with the game's own ships and effects.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-11, quoted in full on the design page: "A cutscene designer is also needed in the mod tool for users to add introduction film and custom animations … Cutscenes always use basic physics so that the animation behavior is predictable. There are both scripted entities and autopilot in the cut scenes … Switching between cameras in the cutscene is set through keyframes." With decision D4: "Also a flag for the animations for their weapons to cause no damage." Decision D3: captions as text keys. Plan item MD6 (the editor) and MD2 (the format and player).
  • Specified by: R-MOD-021, R-MOD-031, R-MOD-032, R-MOD-033, R-MOD-034, R-MOD-035, R-MOD-036, R-MOD-037, R-MOD-038, R-MOD-039, R-MOD-040, R-MOD-041, R-MOD-042, R-MOD-043

docs.title: F-MOD-011 Cutscenes in the game
docs.text:
What. The game plays a pack's cutscenes as the campaign's introduction, at key campaign events, and at the start and end of specific missions (an outro chosen by the result). The player can always skip one with Esc, the tablet console's skip button or the gamepad's Start button.

Why. Story moments in a campaign, the same way every time.

  • Status: in-progress — MD2 (app 0.13.0): cutscenes/<id>.yaml with keyframed scripted craft, timed fire and destruction, fixed and attached cameras, cuts and captions, played as a campaign's introduction and from events, skipped with Esc; the X-COM campaign's films play the same way as Smacker videos. Remaining: autopilot entities, formations, mission intros and outros, skipping from the console or pad
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-11, quoted in full on the design page: "introduction film and custom animations that play for key campaign events or at the start of specific mission definitions". Plan item MD2.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-033, R-MOD-034, R-MOD-035, R-MOD-036, R-MOD-037, R-MOD-038, R-MOD-039, R-MOD-040, R-MOD-041, R-MOD-042, R-MOD-043, R-MOD-044, R-MOD-045

docs.title: F-MOD-012 Video cutscenes
docs.text:
What. A pack can provide a video file to play instead of any engine-played cutscene, with optional captions. Videos play through the operating system's media framework (on Linux, GStreamer when installed); image sequences with a WAV track always work.

Why. A creator may make a film in another program.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-11, quoted in full on the design page: "Note that a user may also provide a video to play instead of scripted engine animation." Decision D2, 2026-11-11 (the Linux path to be evaluated first). Plan item MD3.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-044, R-MOD-045, R-MOD-046

docs.title: F-MOD-013 Shared formations
docs.text:
What. Formations (vee, line abreast, echelon, box, diamond and custom ones) are pack data, used by wingmen in battle and by groups in cutscenes alike.

Why. A modder defines a shape once; a cutscene and a battle look the same.

  • Status: in-progress. Formations are pack data used by wingmen (MD1, app 0.6.6); cutscenes use them with MD2.
  • Source: The user's request, 2026-11-11, quoted in full on the design page: "For fighters and ships, they can choose which formation to apply." Plan item MD1 (it also serves wingmen and replaces per-scenario slot offsets).
  • Specified by: R-MOD-039, R-MOD-047, R-CMB-022

docs.title: F-MOD-014 3D cockpit instrument placement
docs.text:
What. In the Mod Designer, the instruments of a 3D cockpit (radar, MFD, gauges, status, message, power, systems and so on) are placed by dragging each one around the screen over the cockpit model: a ray from the eye through the cursor finds the face below it, and the instrument is previewed applied to that face, at the hit point with the face's normal, at an adjustable size. The result is the cockpit's anchors. A mod extending a pack can create a 3D cockpit from the parent's: the modder picks the cockpit images to extract (copied into the mod, provenance recorded), starts from the parent's 3D model or, if there is none, a generic base cockpit from resources/default, edits it in Blender, then places the instruments.

The first test case for the mod tools is exactly this: a mod extending interceptor with a 3D X-COM cockpit. The user also intends to design an X-COM 3D cockpit in Blender and ship it as an example mod that replaces the 2D cockpit image.

Why. Modding first: a 3D cockpit is only usable when its instruments sit on the right faces, and a modder should not have to measure anchors by hand.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user, 2026-11-11: "for xcom cockpits, we will be designing a 3d cockpit in blender to include as an example mod that substitutes the 3d to replace the 2d image. This raises a point for the mod design tools, they need to accommodate placement of the UI elements so that they are projected onto the correct faces in a 3d view. Simple handling will be to allow each element to be dragged around the screen to detemine their positions and then previewed by applying to the geometry that it is over. this will be the first test case for the mod design tools when available - a mod extending interceptor, where user selects the cockpit images to extract, they are copied into the mod, select to create a 3d cockpit (which will provide a generic base cockpit geometry defined in default if none is present in the parent). The user can then edit it in Blender." Plan items MD8, MD9.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-048, R-MOD-049, R-MOD-050, R-MOD-051, R-MOD-052, R-HUD-004

docs.title: F-MOD-015 Single-file models and Blender sources
docs.text:
What. OBJ/MTL with separate texture files stays a fully supported model format, the one the existing packs use. In addition, a model can be one .glb file (binary glTF: mesh, materials and textures together), read in-crate with no dependency. A mod can also carry its .blend files as the source: the designer exports them to OBJ/MTL or .glb through Blender, run headless when installed; the engine never reads .blend. Every import and export keeps each material with its texture images.

Why. A modder can package a model, its materials and its textures as one file, and keep the Blender source beside it.

  • Status: planned
  • Source: The user, 2026-11-11: "If possible, it would be ideal to allow the .blend files to be included in addtition to standaole mtl and obj objects so that a user can package the object, material, and textures into a single file, but that is not strictly necessary as long as the correct relationshps between materials and their texture images is consistently maintained." Confirmed: "ok that works. obj/mtl as in the existing packs of course would continue to be supported." Plan item MD10.
  • Specified by: R-MOD-053, R-MOD-054, R-MOD-055, R-MOD-010

Why. Escort missions stay interesting and playable: single ships would be destroyed quickly.

Built (app 0.9.2, the user's design): the supply vessel with twelve cargo pods and a point-defence laser; flying an ambushed convoy's escort, the surviving share delivered. docs.title: Game design and mod format
docs.text: Status: design, version 1 draft (2026-11-10). Nothing in this section is implemented yet unless a page says so; the implementation plan schedules it. Pages written here are the reference the stages implement against: a key named here is the key the engine will read.

docs.title: The goal
docs.text:
OpenInterceptor is a general engine for space-combat strategy games: a real-time strategy layer (a star map, bases, research, an economy, factions) wrapped around a first-person space combat simulator. Everything a game is made of is a mod: a folder of rules, campaign definitions, scripts and assets.

Three mods define what "done" means:

Mod Kind What it proves interceptor campaign, needs the player's CD The format can express every system of the original game: the full X-COM: Interceptor campaign is the primary test case. default campaign, original-free The engine stands alone: a complete, smaller campaign — two factions competing for the resources of a few star systems — built only from content made for this project. It ships with the engine and is what runs when no CD is present. interceptor-remastered campaign with parent = interceptor A mod can extend another campaign and override individual assets: sharper textures for modern screens and an upgraded fighter model with real raised and recessed geometry.

docs.title: Pages
docs.text: Page Contents The original game, system by system A functional analysis of X-COM: Interceptor: every system, its rules, and where its data lives. Mod structure Mod kinds, parent, folder layout, load order, ids, overrides, generated assets. Format: campaign and game flow The campaign ruleset: start state, calendar, phases, difficulty, victory and defeat. Format: strategy layer Star map, factions and relations, economy, research, bases and modules, ships, equipment, pilots. Logistics Planned for the default campaign: resources and deposits, mining facilities, research stations, manufacturing centers, supply convoys and ambushes, survey ships, construction stages; open questions. Format: space objects and models Object descriptors, model sets (intact, damage, debris, construction states), mounts. Format: missions and events Mission types and generation, objectives, outcomes; scripted campaign events. Format: behaviours and scripting AI and object behaviours with difficulty variants; the condition/action language; scripts. Format: interface, text and media Screen layouts and skins, cockpits, text and encyclopaedia, music, video. Coverage matrix Every original system → the format construct that expresses it → its simplified equivalent in the default campaign. The Interceptor campaign mod How the interceptor mod defines the full original campaign from the CD. The default campaign Design of the original-free campaign, its content and how its assets are generated. Interceptor Remastered Asset recipes: upscaled textures and mesh patches built locally from the player's CD.

docs.title: Design principles
docs.text:
1. Data first, scripts second. Everything the original game does must be expressible as rules and declarative definitions (with a small condition language). Scripts exist for mods that want behaviour the declarative layer cannot describe; the interceptor and default campaigns must not need them. This keeps campaigns checkable by --check, saves deterministic, and modding approachable.
  2. One format for both campaigns. Every construct the original needs has a simpler use in the default campaign, and vice versa (coverage). A feature only one of them would use is a sign the format is shaped around a game rather than a genre.
  3. Extend what exists. The established conventions stay: YAML rules files (mod format 2, checked against schemas) with inherit (including inherit: original:<file>/<section> to read the original INI data), layering by load order, original: references, per-asset overrides at fixed paths, OBJ/PNG/WAV for mod art. New content types are new top-level sections and folders, not a new syntax.
  4. No original content in the repository. The interceptor mod is rules and references; the remastered mod is recipes that the engine applies to the player's own files.
  5. Everything is validated. Every reference, condition and expression is checked at load (--check) with a message naming the file, line and key path.

docs.title: The default campaign
docs.text:
Status: design; built up stage by stage (plan). First playable content delivered in Stage 2 (resources/default since app 0.4.2, before that packs/default, which replaced the Stage 1 sample pack). Mod id default, kind campaign, no original content. Working title: Perils of the Void.

It is what the engine runs without the player's original data (an installed copy or the CD), the reference implementation of a complete campaign, and the template a modder copies to make their own. It uses every format construct the interceptor campaign uses, in a simpler form (coverage).

docs.title: Aesthetic: a 1950s film serial
docs.text:
The look and the story come from the science-fiction cinema serials and pulp magazine covers of the late 1940s and 1950s — as a genre, not any particular serial or character:

  • Ships: stylised rocket ships (needle and cigar hulls, swept tail fins, nose cones, porthole rows, chrome trim, exhaust bells) against flying saucers (domed discs, rim lights, antenna spikes) and tin-can robots. Low-poly forms with smooth shading and saturated two-tone paint.
  • Palette: rocket-red, cream, chrome and teal for the player; violet, acid green and black for the villain; Technicolor nebulae and painted-backdrop planets with rings.
  • Interface: art-deco panels, Bakelite knobs, radar scopes with phosphor green sweeps, Nixie-tube counters, ticker-tape messages; screen titles in poster lettering.
  • Story: told in chapters. Each opens with a title card ("Chapter 4: Trapped in the Ion Storm!") and a narrator's recap. Each ends on a cliffhanger: a special mission that begins at the worst possible moment. The next chapter resolves it.
  • Planets: battles also happen on worlds — jungle planets under violet skies, airless cratered moons — where rockets fly like aircraft: drag slows them, gravity pulls them down, and fights are slower and closer to the ground (environments).
  • Sound: theremin and organ stings, ray-gun zaps, rocket roars, a brassy title fanfare, all synthesised.

docs.title: Premise
docs.text:
The inner worlds are powered by cosmium, a glowing crystal found only in the asteroid belts and moons of six frontier systems. The Interplanetary Guard (the player) protects the mining colonies. From a dark moon at the edge of the map, Regent Vexor of the Umbral Dominion has begun building the Eclipse Engine: a colossal lens that, fed with enough cosmium, will cast the inner worlds into permanent night unless they kneel.

Both sides race to mine the belts, research new technology, build stations and fight for every system. The Regent needs cosmium for his Engine; the Guard needs it to stop him.

docs.title: Factions
docs.text:
Faction Role Kind Notes Interplanetary Guard The player player Rocket ships; bases with modules Umbral Dominion The opponent; its diabolical plan drives the campaign rival Saucers and robots; own economy, research tree, bases, strategist Solar Senate Third party: the government patron Funds the Guard per protected colony; can cut funding, demand missions, or (if relations collapse) recognise the Regent and stop funding altogether Nebula Cartel Third party: smugglers and traders independent Sells rare parts to whoever pays; secretly supplies the Dominion while relations with the Guard are poor; can be turned into an ally or broken Belt Prospectors Third party: free miners independent Their mines yield cosmium to whoever protects them Black Comet raiders Third party: pirates hostile Raid everyone; may be hired by the Cartel or the Regent

Relations are dynamic (format). Defending a faction's bases, convoys and ships raises its standing with the Guard; attacking them lowers it; and each faction's enemies react the opposite way. Over the campaign the player can make the Cartel an ally (its convoys then supply the Guard and stop supplying the Regent), lose the Senate's backing by neglecting its colonies, or drive the Prospectors into the Regent's arms. Stances change who fights alongside or against the player in battle, who trades, and which story branches open.

docs.title: Structure: chapters driven by both sides' progress
docs.text:
The campaign is one arc of 12 chapters. A chapter's cliffhanger mission is triggered by conditions on the player's progress and the Regent's plan, not by the calendar alone, so a strong player meets the story faster and a struggling one sees the villain advance.

The Eclipse Engine is a plan with three stages (Lens, Coils, Heart). Each stage needs shipments of cosmium and parts carried by saucer convoys, which the player can intercept, and the plan's progress is visible to every chapter condition.

Ch. Title (working) Cliffhanger triggered when Special mission Outcome 1 The Shadow Falls Campaign start Tutorial defence: saucers strike a mining colony Unlocks the star map, first base 2 Raiders of the Belt First mine built, or day 15 Convoy escort through raider space Prospectors' relation; cosmium income 3 The Regent's Ultimatum Dominion builds its 2nd base, or Guard researches 4 topics Broadcast intercept: catch a saucer carrying the Regent's message Reveals the Eclipse Engine; plan stage 1 begins 4 Trapped in the Ion Storm! Plan ≥ 15% and a Guard squadron is in deep space Survive: an ion storm cripples sensors while saucers attack Storm map hazard learned; derelict found 5 The Secret of the Derelict Chapter 4 done Surface salvage: the derelict has crashed on a jungle planet; fly down through the atmosphere and tractor it out under fire from saucers and ground robots Research: saucer propulsion 6 Senate in Peril Senate relation < 20 or plan ≥ 33% Defend the Senate station from a robot boarding fleet Senate relation ±; funding changes 7 The Cartel's Price Cartel relation crosses friendly or wary Choice: escort a Cartel shipment (Cartel ally) or raid it (cut the Regent's supply) Branches: Cartel ally or Cartel hostile 8 Lens of Doom Plan stage 1 complete Strike the lens assembly yard Delays stage 2 (or loses a colony) 9 The Traitor in the Guard Guard researches saucer propulsion and Dominion research ≥ level 2 Pursuit: chase a defector's stolen rocket before it reaches the Regent One rival research topic stolen or kept 10 Into the Dark Moon's Shadow Plan ≥ 66% or Guard holds 4 systems Surface recon: fly low over the dark moon's airless craters, under the fortress guns, to photograph the Engine site Map of the Engine site 11 The Eclipse Begins! Plan stage 3 starts Desperate defence: the Engine fires a test beam at a colony; save its people Colony saved or lost; Senate reaction 12 Duel at the Eclipse Engine Map found + atomic torpedo researched + flagship built Final assault, two parts: break the fleet, then fly into the Engine's core Victory (total or partial)

Victory: destroy the Eclipse Engine (total victory if the flagship survives, partial if it is lost). Defeat: the Engine completes; the Guard's last base falls; or the Senate withdraws recognition (funding at 0 for 60 days).

docs.title: Logistics: mines, research stations and foundries (planned)
docs.text:
Features: Strategy & logistics (F-STR-005 – F-STR-009).

The user has asked for the default campaign's strategy layer to run on supply lines (design; decisions recorded 2026-11-11):

  • New base types: mining facility, research station, manufacturing center, built in star systems according to their resources; research stations only in systems meeting a research site's criteria (a nebula, a pulsar…).
  • Supply and demand: the main base orders components (for fighters and other technology) from manufacturing centers; manufacturing orders materials from mining facilities; nothing is produced until its materials have arrived. Resources and components are campaign data.
  • Supply convoys are automatic, provided by the government, and travel the fixed lanes as convoys of several large vessels (a core vessel with attached cargo containers), each carrying an even share of the cargo, so a partly destroyed convoy still delivers the surviving share. Where along its route a convoy will be attacked is chosen at random at launch; destroyed cargo is lost, captured cargo goes to the Dominion's supply depots (destroy a depot to seize it).
  • Research stations open tech branches that ordinary bases cannot research (for example theremin shielding at a nebula lab); materials are needed only to begin a project.
  • Survey ships — a different mission and craft from supply ships — are sent to systems within the base's radar range to find which station types they suit; when one launches, a 25 % roll decides whether it will be attacked.
  • Fighters are built at main bases and transferred to a facility's own pool, defending it and escorting its supply ships.
  • Construction takes time and passes through three construction stages, each with its own mesh and debris (implemented: build_25 from 0 %, build_60 from 60 %, build_90 from 90 %, thresholds confirmed); from 50 % the Dominion may attack a facility under construction, at most three times per location.
  • Third-party convoys: Prospectors fly expeditions (to a system, pause, home); the Cartel's destinations are random, even uncharted stars.

This fits the premise — both sides race to mine the belts — and gives the Escort and Convoy raid mission types a strategic cause. The Regent's Eclipse Engine shipments use the same convoys. Owners: Stage 4 (economy and logistics), Stage 3 (convoy-ambush and construction-defence missions), Stage 5 (the Dominion's depots and third-party convoys). Already built in Stage 2: the facility and supply-craft objects, their construction-stage models and debris, and the construction-defence and convoy-ambush testbed arenas. Still open: supply-vessel cargo capacity (TBD, set by tech-tree balance) (design page). The interceptor campaign stays without logistics.

docs.title: Generated mission types
docs.text: Type Goal Intercept Destroy a Dominion strike group before it reaches a colony Defend Hold a base, colony, mine or allied station Escort Bring a convoy (prospector, Cartel or Senate) through — and, with logistics, the Guard's own supply rockets (convoy_ambush) Construction defence Hold a facility under construction against a Dominion strike (logistics, planned) Convoy raid Destroy or capture Dominion cargo orbs (slows the Engine) Strike Destroy a Dominion mine, pod or base Patrol Sweep a system; random contacts Salvage Tractor home a disabled saucer or derelict Survey Scan a body to reveal its cosmium Raider hunt Clear a raider nest (relation effects on Cartel and Prospectors) Colony defence (surface) Defend a mining colony or research outpost on a planet: atmospheric flight, gravity, anti-air guns, terrain Ground raid Destroy a Dominion surface mine or research outpost

docs.text:
Asset How Tool Rockets, saucers, robots, stations, modules, probes, mines Procedural low-poly OBJ from parametric parts: lathed hulls (rocket bodies, saucer discs, domes), fins, portholes, antennae, rings; LODs, slots and overlay groups tools/default_assets/models.py (replaced the Stage 1 make_sample_models.py) Debris families Each model cut procedurally into 3–5 pieces along planes, giving the Piece.n models same tool Textures Procedural two-tone paint with chrome trim, rivets, porthole glow, faction insignia, scorch overlays for damage states tools/default_assets/textures.py (PNG, standard library) Cockpits A 3D cockpit per rocket (chrome dash, round dials, radar scope) and one 2D art-deco cockpit image models.py / textures.py UI art Art-deco panels, buttons, dials, chapter title cards, poster-style screen titles, star map glyphs tools/default_assets/ui.py Sounds Synthesised: ray zaps, rocket roar, saucer hum, explosions, theremin and organ stings, UI clicks tools/default_assets/sounds.py (WAV) Music A title fanfare, an exploration loop and a battle loop, synthesised sounds.py Text Chapter cards and narrator recaps, briefings, encyclopaedia, messages, names: written for the project in a pulp register, in text/en/ by hand

All tools are Python standard library only and deterministic (fixed seeds); their outputs are committed so the mod works without running them. Everything is MIT-licensed with the engine. Names, characters and designs are original to this project; the serial genre is the inspiration, not any specific work.

docs.title: F-CPN-001 Choose a campaign
docs.text:
What. One campaign is played at a time, chosen on the command line, in the settings or in the launcher; its addons come with it.

Why. Modding first: a campaign is the unit a modder ships.

  • Source: Plan item 2.1.
  • Specified by: R-CPN-001

docs.title: F-CPN-002 Difficulty levels
docs.text:
What. Each campaign defines its difficulty levels; the player picks one, and it is remembered per campaign.

Why. The original has five levels; the default campaign has four.

  • Status: implemented
  • Source: Plan items 2.8 and 2.23.
  • Specified by: R-CPN-002

docs.title: F-CPN-003 The default campaign, Perils of the Void
docs.text:
What. A complete, smaller campaign made only from content made for this project, playable with no CD: rockets against saucers in a 1950s film serial.

Why. Modding first: proves the engine stands alone and is the worked example for modders.

  • Status: in-progress — rules, scenarios, nine missions (five using environments, hazards and ground installations, app 0.6.4), radio voices (app 0.6.2); the strategy layer and logistics (app 0.7.1 – 0.9.0); flown convoy battles (0.9.2); the 12-chapter serial with the Eclipse Engine plan, relations, endings and the finale eclipse_assault (0.10.1) — chapters 1 – 11 still fly existing missions; not played through.

docs.title: F-CPN-004 The Interceptor campaign
docs.text:
What. The full X-COM: Interceptor campaign, played from the player's CD.

Why. Compatibility, and the primary test that the formats can express every system of the original.

  • Status: in-progress — 26 mission types (app 0.6.5) and the strategy layer from the player's data, derived and not yet play-tested (app 0.8.0); the Doomsday arc and plan, MacArthur and the final mission, two of seven side missions (app 0.10.2, derived gates); the Think.ini strategist remains; not played through.

docs.title: F-CPN-005 Interceptor Remastered
docs.text:
What. A campaign that extends Interceptor, with sharper textures and an upgraded fighter model generated from the player's data.

Why. Proves a mod can extend another campaign and override individual assets.

docs.title: F-CPN-006 Story, rivals and relations
docs.text:
What. Events, story arcs, a rival with its own plans and strategist, factions whose relations change, and endings.

Why. What turns the strategy layer into a campaign with a beginning, middle and end.
