docs.title: Running
docs.text:
cargo test                     # all
cargo test sim::               # one module
cargo test proximity           # tests whose name contains "proximity"
cargo test -- --nocapture      # show println! output

docs.title: Workflows
docs.text: How work is done in this project, following SpecItOut.

docs.title: Issues
docs.text: Issues are reached only through the sio client (sio issues list | show | create | comment …), with SPECITOUT_ACTOR set. The forge is GitHub: the repository is public at github.com/bbogovich/OpenInterceptor and issues are GitHub Issues, which the client syncs (sio issues sync); nothing else writes them. Labels: formats, packs, flight, combat, render, input, testbed, campaign, platform, docs.

docs.title: Rapid Prototyping
docs.text:
The project follows the Rapid Prototyping workflow (a SpecItOut proposal, P65; not yet supported by the sio client). The definition and the specification live on this site: version 1.0.0 from 2026-11-11, 1.1.0 since the interlude's playtest fixes (app 0.3.1), 1.2.0 with the resources/ folder (F-CMP-005), 1.3.0 with console C1 (app 0.4.0), 1.4.0 – 1.6.0 with the console heartbeat, collisions and Simple physics, and 1.7.0 with the planned Mod Designer, Cutscene Designer and game bundling (MD1–MD7) and the console's pairing fix and keep-awake.

  1. Each user request, in the same pass and before any code:
    1. a feature (F-<AREA>-NNN) is created or updated on the definition page for its area;
    2. requirements (R-<AREA>-NNN) citing that feature are written or revised on the specification page for the area;
    3. issues are queued in sio, citing the requirements.
  2. No approval gates. The definition and the specification are a permanent record: IDs are never reused, and each page's revision history and the change history record every change.
  3. The specification moves before the code, so no spec sync is needed: code is written against requirements that already say what it must do. Requirements written from code that predates this workflow are marked Reverse-engineered: yes.
  4. When the prototype is complete, the definition and specification seed a formal definition and specification for a production version built through the SpecItOut fast track.

Until sio supports a prototype kind, the manifest stays kind: implementation with spec pointing at this worktree's docs/specification (DEV-042).

docs.title: Specification revision (before 2026-11-11)
docs.text: Before the definition and specification were bootstrapped there was no specification (specVersion: null) and work was implementation-first: each stage was planned on this site and pages cited plan stages. Requirements for that work were written afterwards from the code and are marked Reverse-engineered: yes.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
1. Pick the next item from the current stage; its issue cites the requirements it implements.
  2. Write the code with its unit tests and module documentation (commenting standard).
  3. Update the matching architecture page while implementing.
  4. Run scripts/check.sh; it must pass.
  5. Add manual test cases for anything only a playtest can confirm (manual tests).
  6. Update implementation status and the revision history.

docs.title: Bug resolution
docs.text: A bug is filed as a bug issue with steps to reproduce (scenario ID and ship from the testbed help). Diagnosis is a comment naming the cause; the fix lands with a unit test that fails before the fix, or a new manual case when only a playtest can show it.

docs.title: A stage is complete when
docs.text:
• Every module has unit tests (testing policy),
  • every Stage manual case has been run and recorded as passed,
  • the testbed has the stage's scenarios,
  • and these pages describe what was actually built.

docs.title: Learning
docs.text:
OpenInterceptor's second objective is to be a teaching example: how to build a 3D application and game engine in Rust with sound architecture, coding patterns and data-model design. This section collects the teaching material.

Section Status Contents Learn Rust with this codebase Written The Rust needed to read the engine, page by page Best practices Written The practices the code follows, and why Game design Planned — Mathematics Planned — Physics Planned — Engine Planned — Networking Started The WebSocket handshake and frame masking, defensive limits, threads and channels (the tablet console)

docs.title: Best practices
docs.text:
A secondary goal of OpenInterceptor is to be a worked example of Rust practice for a 3D application or game engine. These pages state the practices the code follows, and why. Code review checks them; where the code falls short, that is a bug.

Page Covers Architectural design Layering, data-driven design, sim/render separation, fixed timestep Coding patterns Newtype ids, plain-data structs, explicit GPU ownership, no global mutable state, error types per layer Data model and performance SoA vs AoS, index handles, baked meshes, LOD, no per-frame allocation, precision Dependency policy Why only macroquad (plus two crates it already includes), and how another would be justified Commenting standard //!, ///, and comments on non-obvious lines Testing policy Unit tests for all code; manual cases for playtest-only behaviour

docs.title: Layering
docs.text:
formats → model → content → sim → input/platform → render/hud/audio → app   (+ check, cli)

The order is written at the top of src/lib.rs.

Each layer depends only on layers to its left. Consequences:

  • formats is pure functions on bytes: testable with hand-made inputs, reusable by tools.
  • sim knows nothing about drawing or windows: testable, deterministic, and usable headless (for AI duels, replays, a future server).
  • Presentation reads the simulation; it never changes it except through Controls.

docs.title: Data-driven design
docs.text: The engine contains no game content. Ships, weapons, stations, cockpits and scenarios come from packs. A quick test for a change: could a modder do this with a pack? If the answer requires editing Rust, ask whether a rule key should exist instead. This is what makes the Interceptor content "just one pack" and a custom campaign possible.

docs.title: Separate simulation from rendering
docs.text:
flowchart LR
    I["input → Controls"] --> S["sim::World::step (60 Hz)"]
    S --> R["render + hud (every display frame)"]

The simulation is the single source of truth. Rendering is a view of it. The player and the AI both drive ships through the same Controls, so the AI obeys the same flight model, and the simulation reports what happened as SimEvents that effects, sound and the message line consume — none of which can change the battle.

docs.title: Fixed timestep
docs.text: The simulation advances in constant 1/60 s steps, run as many times as needed per display frame (see the loop). Physics and AI then behave the same on a 60 Hz laptop and a 144 Hz monitor, and a recorded input sequence replays identically.

docs.title: One owner per resource
docs.text: Each long-lived resource has one owner: the AppContext owns the Content (packs, original data, rules, scenarios), the Renderer (shaders, model and texture caches), the SoundBank and the Bindings; a FlightSession owns its World. Everything else borrows. Shared, read-only data uses reference counting where several owners really exist: the World shares the Ruleset and collision shapes through Arc, ships of one class share a GpuModel through Rc.

docs.title: Errors are values, diagnostics are collected
docs.text: Loading returns Results and collects warnings; nothing in the content path panics on bad data.

docs.title: Commenting standard
docs.text: The code is meant to be read by people learning Rust and game engines, so it explains itself.

docs.title: Every module starts with //!
docs.text:
A module-level doc comment says what the module is for, in terms a beginner can follow, and where it sits in the layers:

//! XMSH mesh reader.
//!
//! Every 3D model in X-COM: Interceptor (ships, stations, asteroids) is an `XMSH` resource
//! inside `xobjects1.dll` / `xobjects2.dll`. This module turns those bytes into a [`Mesh`]:
//! up to four levels of detail, each with vertices, polygons and texture names.
//!
//! Layer: formats (pure functions on bytes; no files, no GPU).
//! Format reference: docs site → Original game → Formats → XMSH meshes.

docs.title: Every public item has ///
docs.text:
Structs, enums, functions, fields that are not self-evident: what it is, units, and what the caller must know.

/// Maximum forward speed in metres per second (`MaxSpeed` in the original rules).
pub max_speed: f32,

docs.title: Comment non-obvious lines
docs.text:
Say why, not what. Units, coordinate conversions, format quirks, invariants:

// Original meshes are Direct3D (left-handed): flip Z and reverse the winding so faces stay
// front-facing in our right-handed frame.
let p = Vec3::new(v.x, v.y, -v.z);

docs.title: SAFETY: on every unsafe
docs.text: See FFI and unsafe.

docs.title: Keep comments true
docs.text: A wrong comment is worse than none. Change the comment in the same commit as the code. cargo doc renders all //! and /// comments into browsable documentation.

docs.title: Data model and performance
docs.text: A 1998 space sim is light work for a modern machine; these practices keep it that way as mods add content, and they are the habits a larger engine needs.

docs.title: Pre-baked GPU meshes per texture
docs.text: At load, each model LOD is converted once (Model::from_xmsh / from_obj, then render::gpu::split_lod) into one chunk per texture: triangle lists with u16 indices. Drawing is then one draw_mesh per chunk, with no parsing or triangulation per frame.

docs.title: Flattened arrays instead of per-item allocations
docs.text: An XMSH polygon does not own a Vec of its vertex indices. All polygons' indices go into one shared Lod::polygon_vertices: Vec<u32>, and each Polygon stores first and count into it. Thousands of tiny heap allocations become one, and iterating polygons reads contiguous memory. ObjMesh does the same with face corners.

docs.title: LOD selection
docs.text: Each original model has four LODs with switch distances from the file (e.g. 75, 150, 450 m and "always" for the Lightning II; 4.2, 8.4, 25 km for the X-COM base). GpuModel::lod(distance) picks the first LOD whose switch distance exceeds the camera distance, cutting triangle counts for distant objects several-fold (the base goes from 659 to 126 polygons).

docs.title: Camera-relative precision
docs.text: Positions are f32 metres. Before drawing, the camera position is subtracted on the CPU (SpaceCamera::model_matrix), and the view matrix is rotation-only, so the camera sits at the origin of render space: nearby geometry is precise and does not jitter even tens of kilometres out.

docs.title: No per-frame allocation
docs.text: The glow and sky geometry is rebuilt every frame into Vecs owned by the Renderer. They are clear()ed (which keeps capacity), moved into a Mesh with std::mem::take, drawn, and moved back — so after the first frame they allocate nothing. In World::step the ruleset is reached through a cloned Arc rather than by cloning a ship class per ship per tick. Remaining small per-frame allocations (HUD text, engine-glow attachment lists) are known and cheap; they are candidates if profiling ever shows them.

docs.title: Index handles instead of references
docs.text: Ships refer to their target by ShipId, not by &Ship. References into a Vec would block mutation of the Vec (borrow rules) and dangle if it reallocated; indices do neither, and they serialise naturally for saves.

docs.title: Structure of arrays where it matters
docs.text: Everything in Stage 1 is an array of structs (Vec<Ship>, Vec<Bolt>, Vec<Star>): counts are tens to a few thousand, and AoS is the simplest. Where counts grow large and a hot loop touches only one field, a structure of arrays (positions: Vec<Vec3>, ages: Vec<f32>) reads contiguous memory and is the next step. Choose by measuring, not by habit.

docs.title: Measure first
docs.text: Optimise what a profiler shows, and keep the simple version when it is fast enough. A developer overlay with frame time, draw calls and triangle counts is planned (Stage 2); until then, the model viewer reports triangles per LOD and macOS Instruments or perf profile the release build.

docs.title: Dependency policy
docs.text: Third-party dependencies are avoided by default. One is added only when it solves a problem that would be prohibitively expensive to build here. Every dependency is a liability carried forever: it changes without our requirements, may be abandoned, and pulls in its own tree.

docs.title: Before adding one, state
docs.text:
• Feature complexity — genuinely hard, or just unfamiliar?
  • Stability — release history, maintenance, number of maintainers.
  • Its dependency tree — the transitive weight is part of the cost.
  • How much would be used — a large crate for one function is never justified.
  • Licence — MIT/Apache/BSD/zlib. Never GPL; LGPL only with great care.

The evaluation is recorded here before the dependency is added (a project rule in CLAUDE.md). Versions are pinned exactly (=x.y.z) so an upstream release cannot change the build silently; Cargo.lock is committed.

docs.title: Current dependencies (Cargo.toml)
docs.text: Crate Features Why macroquad =0.4.14 default + audio Window, OpenGL context, input, textures, 2D/3D drawing, sound playback. glam =0.27.0 default Vectors, matrices, quaternions for model, sim and render. image =0.24.9 png only Decoding PNG textures in mod packs; encoding PNG for the extractor, --screenshot and (since main 2ed1149) the console's target textures.

docs.title: Evaluation
docs.text:
Question macroquad glam image (png) Feature complexity Cross-platform windowing, GL contexts, input and audio back-ends are genuinely hard and platform-specific. 3D maths is not hard, but a correct, fast, well-tested quaternion/matrix library is a lot of code to own. PNG needs DEFLATE plus filters and chunk handling: modest but not worth owning. Stability Used by ArenaVM and Looking Glass on this machine with the same pinned version; maintained since 2020. Very widely used, stable API, active maintenance. Long-lived, widely used. Dependency tree miniquad, fontdue, glam, image (png, tga), quad-rand; the audio feature adds quad-snd (CoreAudio on macOS, ALSA on Linux — the Linux build needs libasound2-dev) and its small decoders. None added: already in macroquad's tree at exactly this version. None added: already in macroquad's tree at this version with the png feature. How much is used Most of what we use from it is core (window, input, drawing, materials, audio). Most of Vec2/Vec3/Vec4/Quat/Mat4. One function: load_from_memory_with_format. Justified only because it costs nothing extra. Licence MIT / Apache-2.0 MIT / Apache-2.0 MIT / Apache-2.0

glam and image are used directly (rather than through macroquad's re-exports) so that the content and sim layers do not depend on the windowing library — they compile and are tested without it in mind — at zero added build weight.

docs.title: Built in-crate instead
docs.text:
PE resources, XMSH, XTXR, TGA, WAV (PCM, MS ADPCM, IMA ADPCM), INI, OBJ/MTL, command-line parsing, the gamepad layers (Objective-C shim compiled by build.rs; Linux joystick API with std), random numbers for AI and effects, the starfield, and since Stage 2 the YAML reader and writer, the schema validator and JSON Schema exporter, and the condition language (lexer, parser, type checker, evaluator). Each is a few hundred lines with tests.

YAML, evaluated (Stage 2). Mod files moved to YAML. The usual crate, serde_yaml, is unmaintained (archived by its author), and alternatives would bring serde and a YAML engine into the tree for a small part of what they do. Full YAML also behaves in ways that surprise modders (implicit typing such as no → false, anchors and aliases). The project's files need mappings, lists, scalars, block text and comments — about 750 lines in formats::yaml, with every value kept as text until the schema types it, so errors can name the file, line and key. Decision: build in-crate (DEV-030).

Console networking, evaluated (C1, app 0.4.0). The tablet console needs an HTTP server, the WebSocket protocol, SHA-1 and base64 for its handshake, and JSON. The usual crates (tungstenite or an async web framework, sha1, base64, serde_json) would bring in serde, often an async runtime, and their trees — for a server that serves three embedded files and exchanges small JSON messages with one or two tablets. Only a fraction would be used: no TLS, no keep-alive, no chunking, no request bodies, no fragmented messages. Written in-crate: remote::http (~120 lines), remote::ws with SHA-1 and base64 (~260, tested against the FIPS and RFC vectors), remote::json (~360) and threads from std. Decision: build in-crate; no dependency added. The console page itself (web/console/) is plain custom elements and CSS with no framework or build step.

Smacker video, evaluated (Stage 6.3, app 0.12.0). The original's films and talking heads are Smacker files. The alternatives were a C library bound by FFI (the widely used open decoder is part of FFmpeg, LGPL — the licence trap the policy warns of, and a large native build for one codec), a third-party Rust crate (one more dependency, with its own maintenance risk, for a single format), or the operating system's media frameworks (which do not read Smacker). The format is publicly described and small: a bit reader, two kinds of Huffman tree with a three-value cache, four block types, a delta palette and DPCM audio. Written in-crate: formats::smacker, about 600 lines with its comments, plus tests on hand-built bitstreams (and formats::mpsrc, ~80 lines, for the pack the talking heads come in), checked by hand against all eleven videos on the reference CD. Decision: build in-crate; no dependency added. Video files in other formats for mods (MD3) are still to be evaluated: the plan is the platform's own frameworks behind the platform shim, with GStreamer on Linux only through dlopen — that evaluation goes on this page before MD3 is built (R-MOD-046).

Music, skins and cutscenes (app 0.11.0 – 0.13.0) needed nothing new either: music is WAV playback through macroquad's audio with lengths from formats::wav; skins use macroquad's textures and its TrueType font loader; the default music and panel art are generated by Python scripts using only the standard library; the cutscene splines are a few lines of glam.

docs.title: PNG encoding: the image crate already in the tree
docs.text: Resolved (main 2ed1149, after app 0.9.0). The console's textured target model sends each texture as a PNG data: URL, so the game must write PNG. App 0.6.7 wrote it in-crate (formats::png, about 140 lines: stored deflate blocks, a bit-by-bit CRC-32 and an Adler-32), and the last review of this page noted that this duplicated a capability already in the tree: the image crate above is a direct dependency with its png feature, which encodes as well as decodes, and the extractor and --screenshot already used it. The duplicate is gone: formats::png::encode_rgba now calls image::codecs::png::PngEncoder, and the module keeps only the downscaling the console needs. No dependency was added or removed — Cargo.toml is unchanged — and the images are now compressed. The policy point it illustrates: before writing something in-crate, check whether a crate already in the tree does it; keeping a second copy is a cost without the benefit of avoiding a dependency.

docs.title: External tools
docs.text:
Programs the user may have installed, which the project calls but never links, bundles or requires, are not dependencies.

Blender (planned, MD10). A mod may carry .blend files as the source of its models. When Blender is installed, the Mod Designer runs it headless on save (blender -b file.blend --python-expr …) to export OBJ/MTL or .glb; without it, the exported files already in the pack are used. The engine never parses .blend, whose binary format changes between Blender versions. Blender is GPL, but it runs as a separate program on the user's own files and nothing of it enters the codebase. See R-MOD-054.

.glb (planned, MD10) is read in-crate: the glTF JSON chunk with remote::json and the binary buffers; no crate is added (R-MOD-053).

docs.title: Tier 2 scripting, evaluated (Stage 3.10) — awaiting the user's decision
docs.text:
Awaiting the user's decision

This is the evaluation R-MOD-015 asks for before a second-tier script language is added. No decision has been made. The recommendation below is the evaluator's; the user decides. Nothing is added to Cargo.toml until then. GitHub issue #16.

The question. Tier 1 — behaviours as state machines, missions as definitions, and the checked condition and action language (script::*) — carries both shipped campaigns. Tier 2 is for what Tier 1 cannot express: logic with memory and branching, such as a boss with phases, a custom ending, or an event chain that counts and remembers (Format: behaviours and scripting › Tier 2). Whatever the language, the design already fixes its contract: scripts are called through hooks, see only the documented query and action API, run on the 60 Hz simulation tick, are deterministic (no clock, files or network; random numbers only from the game's generator) and keep state only through the API, so a save never serialises a script VM.

Three options:

  • (a) mlua — Rust bindings to Lua 5.4 (or LuaJIT, or Luau), building the Lua C sources that it bundles (the vendored feature).
  • (b) rhai — an embedded scripting language written in Rust.
  • (c) Grow script::* — extend the in-crate condition and action language into a small statement language: local variables, if / else, bounded loops, functions, and calls into the same checked queries and actions.

What could not be verified. This evaluation was written without network access. Release history, maintainer counts and dependency trees below are from the evaluator's knowledge of the crates up to 2025, marked (unverified); before adding either crate, check them on crates.io and the repositories, and record the exact version and cargo tree output here. The lines-of-code figures for (c) are counted from main 90653b9; the estimate of its growth is derived.

Question (a) mlua (b) rhai (c) grow script::* Feature complexity A full language VM — garbage collector, coroutines, tables, closures, standard library — is genuinely hard; so is a safe binding over Lua's C API (errors that longjmp, userdata lifetimes, panics across the FFI boundary). Not something to build here. The same scope in pure Rust: parser, AST optimiser, closures, modules, a dynamic value type. Genuinely hard to build, but more than Tier 2 needs. Modest, and the hard parts exist: the lexer, recursive-descent parser, type checker and evaluator are ~540 lines in script/mod.rs, with the battle and object contexts (~160 lines each) and actions (~150). Statements, scopes, a call stack and an operation budget add an estimated 800 – 1 200 lines with tests (derived). The expensive part is design and documentation, not code. Stability Lua 5.4 itself: decades of slow, careful releases from a three-person team at PUC-Rio. mlua: a 2019 fork of rlua, still 0.x — its minor releases (0.9 → 0.10 → 0.11) have changed the API (unverified). One principal maintainer: bus factor ≈ 1 (unverified). LuaJIT is effectively one maintainer and stops at Lua 5.1 semantics. 1.x since 2021 with frequent releases that have kept 1.x compatible (unverified). Started by one author, maintained for several years mainly by one other in the rhaiscript organisation: bus factor ≈ 1 (unverified). Ours. It changes only when this project changes it; no upstream can break the build. The cost is that we carry it forever. Transitive tree mlua-sys plus lua-src (or luajit-src) for the bundled C sources; at build time cc and pkg-config, and a C compiler on every platform (macOS already needs one for the gamepad shim; Linux and Windows builders would too). A handful of small Rust crates besides (for example bstr, num-traits, rustc-hash) (unverified). C code in the process; cross-compiling and a WebAssembly build (macroquad can target the web) become harder. Pure Rust, but several crates: for example ahash (with getrandom, once_cell, zerocopy), smartstring, thin-vec, num-traits, bitflags, a time crate, and the procedural macro crate rhai_codegen with syn, quote, proc-macro2 — roughly 15 – 20 crates and noticeably longer clean builds (unverified). None. How much would be used A small fraction: one VM state, a dozen registered functions, a few userdata types, limits. Not async, serde, modules, the C module loader or most of the standard library. A small fraction: Engine, compile to AST, registered functions, limits. Not modules, serde, metadata, the optimiser's levels or the codegen macros beyond registration. All of it, by construction: only what modders need is built. Licence mlua MIT; Lua 5.4 MIT; LuaJIT MIT; Luau MIT. MIT OR Apache-2.0. The project's own (MIT). Sandboxing Possible but opt-in: load only safe libraries (no io, os, package, debug, load of bytecode), a memory limit, an instruction-count hook to stop runaway scripts. The VM is C: a bug there or in the binding is memory-unsafe in our process. Determinism needs care: Lua uses f64 where the simulation uses f32, and pairs() order over string-keyed tables depends on a per-state hash seed that Lua 5.4 randomises by default (derived) — replays could diverge unless that is controlled. Good: no file, network or clock access unless registered; limits on operations, call depth, string, array and map sizes, and a progress callback to abort. Memory-safe Rust. Maps are ordered, so iteration is deterministic (unverified). Errors such as calling an unknown function surface at run time, not at load. By construction: the only effects are the actions in the checked table, the only inputs the documented queries, values are f32 like the simulation, and there is no I/O to remove. Every name, argument and type is checked when the files load, as conditions are today; an operation budget per hook call guarantees that a loop finishes. Modder experience Lua is the most widely known game-modding language; editors, tutorials and debuggers exist. Rust-like syntax; few modders know it; good error messages. One language from condition to script: a modder who writes hull < 25% today writes if hull < 25% { message(@msg.retreat) } tomorrow, and --check catches mistakes before play. No outside tutorials or debugger; the docs site must teach it. Performance Fast (LuaJIT very fast). A tree-walking interpreter, several times slower than Lua (unverified); fine for hooks, poor for per-tick logic on many ships. Like today's conditions: a tree walk over pre-resolved query indices with no allocation. Fast enough for hooks; not a general-purpose fast path. Teaching value (objective 2) Shows FFI and embedding, which platform already shows. Shows embedding a Rust library. Shows how an interpreter grows from expressions to statements, scopes and a call stack — a classic exercise, in code already documented for beginners.

What (c) would be. A small statement language over the same checked API, not a general-purpose one:

# a hook body (illustrative syntax, not a decided design)
let shots = 0
if hull < 25% and not system_damaged(engines) {
    message(@msg.guardian_enraged)
    for each member of guards { order(member, attack_player) }
} else {
    shots = shots + 1
}
def enraged() { return hull < 25% }
  • Local variables (numbers, true/false, names) live for one hook call; anything that must last goes through actions (set_flag, counters, object variables), as the design requires.
  • Loops are bounded: over a role's members or a counted range, plus an operation budget per call.
  • Functions are defined in the pack and checked for their arguments; no recursion (or a fixed depth).
  • Strings, tables, closures and libraries are deliberately out of scope.

Its ceiling. (c) cannot host what needs general-purpose data structures or algorithms: a procedural generator, a custom AI planner, string processing, a mod's own data tables. If mods need that, a real language is needed, and the choice between (a) and (b) comes back.

docs.title: Recommendation (the evaluator's; awaiting the user)
docs.text:
1. Default: (c), grow script::*. Under the dependency policy a dependency is added only when building the feature here would be prohibitively expensive. It would not be: the lexer, parser, checker and evaluator exist; mods already use the language; it is checked at load, deterministic and sandboxed by construction; and it adds nothing to the tree. Both shipped campaigns need only Tier 1, so the extension can be built when a mod first needs it.
  2. Fallback: (a), mlua with Lua 5.4 (vendored), if mods turn out to need a full general-purpose language. Lua is what modders know, it is fast, and its C core is among the most stable code there is; the costs — a C build, an FFI boundary, opt-in sandboxing and the determinism care above — are known and containable behind the same hook API. It would need the version, cargo tree and the sandbox and determinism settings recorded here first.
  3. (b) rhai is not recommended now: it costs more crates than (a) for a language few modders know, with run-time rather than load-time errors. It is the option to reconsider if a pure-Rust or WebAssembly build becomes a requirement, where (a)'s C code is the obstacle.

Whatever is chosen, the hook API is the same, so a Tier 1 definition that calls a hook does not change if the language behind it does.

docs.title: Newtype ids
docs.text:
// src/content/rules.rs
#[derive(Debug, Clone, Copy, PartialEq, Eq, Hash)]
pub struct ShipClassId(pub u16);

Ids are small, Copy, and typed: a BeamId cannot be confused with a MissileId. Ships are created and destroyed, so their id carries a generation and a stale id is detected:

// src/sim/mod.rs
pub struct ShipId { pub index: u32, pub generation: u32 }

pub fn get(&self, id: ShipId) -> Option<&Ship> {
    let i = id.index as usize;
    (self.generations.get(i) == Some(&id.generation)).then(|| &self.ships[i]).filter(|s| s.alive)
}

docs.title: Plain-data structs
docs.text:
Prefer structs with public fields and no hidden behaviour for data that is just data (Controls, ShipClass, Bolt, Placement). Construct with struct literals and ..Default::default():

let c = Controls { throttle_set: Some(1.0), fire_beams: true, ..Default::default() };

A constructor function is used only when construction has rules to enforce (e.g. World::from_scenario, which validates every placement and resolves leaders).

docs.title: Explicit ownership of GPU resources
docs.text: GPU meshes and textures are owned by the Renderer's ModelCache, keyed by asset reference and pack. Drawing code borrows an Rc<GpuModel> for the frame; nothing else holds a Texture2D long-term except the flight session's cockpit image.

docs.title: No global mutable state
docs.text: No static mut, no lazily-initialised global singletons for engine state. State is passed in: renderer.draw_world(&content, &world, &effects, &cam, sun, hide). This keeps functions testable and makes data flow visible in signatures. (macroquad itself keeps a global context for the window; we treat it as the platform and touch it only in presentation code.)

docs.title: Error types per layer
docs.text: FormatError in formats (an enum, because callers can branch on it). Above it, errors are only ever shown to people, so they are Strings built with context (map_err(|e| format!("mesh {name}: {e}"))): messages read as a path from the user's action down to the byte. A typed error enum is introduced the day a caller needs to branch on one.

docs.title: Small functions with names that say what they do
docs.text: flight::turn_factor(speed, lock_speed), targeting::nearest_hostile(world, me), hud::radar_point(local, front), app::flight::view_pose(view, …). Pure helpers are free functions so they can be unit tested without constructing a world or a window.

docs.title: Separate logic from presentation inside a module
docs.text: Where a module must draw, the decisions are pure functions and the drawing is a thin layer on top: hud::mfd_lines (tested) vs hud::draw::draw_instruments (painted); app::launcher::Menu (tested) vs Launcher::draw.

docs.title: Enums over flags
docs.text: enum LinkMode { Linked, Full, Unlinked } rather than two booleans; enum Pilot { External, Ai(AiState) } so AI memory exists only for AI ships — impossible states cannot be represented.

docs.title: Testing policy
docs.text:
1. All code has unit tests before its stage is complete. Readers, rules, flight maths, weapons, targeting, AI decisions, bindings parsing — anything that can run without a window.
  2. Behaviour only a playtest can show (how flight feels, whether the cockpit lines up, whether a gamepad works) gets documented manual test cases in Manual tests, run and recorded before the stage is complete.
  3. Original data is never a test fixture in the repository. Unit tests build their own inputs; checks against real data run through --check when the data is present.
  4. A bug fix comes with a test that fails before the fix (or a manual case if it is playtest-only).
  5. The gate passes on every commit: scripts/check.sh.

Design for testability: pure functions for maths, World::step independent of the window, Controls as plain data so AI and input can be tested the same way.

docs.title: Worked example: turn velocity and changing frames
docs.text: Two playtest fixes rest on the same two ideas: the velocity of a point on a turning body, and moving a vector between the world's axes and the ship's own axes.

docs.title: A point on a turning body moves at ω × r
docs.text:
A ship turning at angular velocity ω (a vector along the turn axis, its length the rate in radians per second) carries every point on it around that axis. A point at offset r from the centre moves at

v = ω × r (the cross product)

On a ship yawing left (ω points up, +Y), a gun on the right wing (r points right, +X) has ω × r = (0, 1, 0) × (1, 0, 0) = (0, 0, −1): it swings forwards (the engine's forward is −Z). A gun 3 m out on a ship yawing at 1 rad/s moves at 3 m/s from the turn alone.

A shot that leaves the gun physically starts with the gun's whole velocity: the ship's own velocity, plus ω × r, plus its muzzle speed along the barrel. That is what sim::combat::fire_beams computes:

let spin = rot * s.angular_velocity;           // ω in world axes (see below)
let offset = rot * mount_offset(k, n, radius); // r, in world axes
let velocity = vel + spin.cross(offset) + dir * beam.speed;

docs.title: Body axes and world axes
docs.text:
The ship's orientation is a unit quaternion rot. Multiplying a vector by it, rot * v, turns a vector written in the ship's axes (x right, y up, −z forward) into world axes. The reverse turn is the conjugate, rot.conjugate() * v: for a unit quaternion the conjugate is the inverse, and it is cheaper to compute (negate three components) than a general inverse.

  • angular_velocity is stored in body axes ("yawing left" is the same vector whichever way the ship faces), so the code turns it into world axes with rot * before the cross product.
  • The HUD's drift readout needs the opposite: the world velocity seen from the ship. Ship::body_velocity is rot.conjugate() * velocity, with z negated so forward reads positive. A ship flying at 300 m/s that yaws 90° keeps its motion (newtonian flight), so in its own axes the same velocity is now 300 m/s sideways: the readout shows X-300 or X+300, depending on the direction of the turn.

The same pair appears in the arcade option bolt_frame: ship: a shot's offset and velocity are stored in its owner's axes (rot.conjugate() *) and placed back into the world each tick with the owner's current orientation (owner.rotation *), so the shot turns with the nose.

Where to look: src/sim/combat.rs (fire_beams, move_bolts), src/sim/mod.rs (Ship::body_velocity), and the tests a_bolt_leaves_with_the_muzzles_velocity_then_flies_straight and body_velocity_reads_drift_in_the_ships_own_axes, which check these formulas with numbers.

docs.title: Networking
docs.text:
Networking taught from OpenInterceptor's own code. The first worked example is the tablet control console (src/remote/, app 0.4.0): a game that serves a web page and a WebSocket to a tablet on the local network, with every protocol layer written in the crate. How the pieces fit is on Remote console; this page explains the protocol mechanics.

More sections (the protocol's design, latency and rates, a serial transport) will follow as the console grows.

docs.title: The WebSocket handshake
docs.text:
A browser cannot open a raw TCP socket. What it can do is send an HTTP request and ask for the connection to be upgraded to a WebSocket (RFC 6455). The tablet's page does this with new WebSocket("ws://<host>/ws"), which sends:

GET /ws HTTP/1.1
Host: 192.168.1.20:8765
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Key: dGhlIHNhbXBsZSBub25jZQ==
Sec-WebSocket-Version: 13

Sec-WebSocket-Key is 16 random bytes in base64, new for every connection. The server must prove that it understood the request as a WebSocket upgrade — not, say, a plain web server that echoes headers back — by transforming the key in a fixed way:

  1. append the fixed GUID 258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11 (the same for every server);
  2. take the SHA-1 of that text;
  3. encode the 20-byte digest in base64.
// src/remote/ws.rs
const GUID: &str = "258EAFA5-E914-47DA-95CA-C5AB0DC85B11";

pub fn accept_key(client_key: &str) -> String {
    base64(&sha1(format!("{}{GUID}", client_key.trim()).as_bytes()))
}

and answer with status 101:

HTTP/1.1 101 Switching Protocols
Upgrade: websocket
Connection: Upgrade
Sec-WebSocket-Accept: s3pPLMBiTxaQ9kYGzzhZRbK+xOo=

For the key above, RFC 6455 §1.3 gives exactly that accept value, so the unit test remote::ws::sha1_and_base64_match_the_published_test_vectors checks accept_key against it, along with SHA-1's FIPS 180 examples and base64's RFC 4648 examples. Test vectors from the standard are the cheapest way to know a hand-written algorithm is right.

SHA-1 is no longer safe for signatures, but here it is only a checksum that proves the server read the key; that use is unaffected. From the 101 response on, the same TCP connection carries WebSocket frames instead of HTTP.

In the code. remote::http::parse_request reads the request head up to the blank line (\r\n\r\n) — returning Ok(None) while it has not all arrived, because TCP delivers a stream of bytes, not messages — and Request::is_websocket checks the method, the Upgrade header and the key. remote::server::serve then writes http::upgrade_response(&ws::accept_key(key)).

docs.title: Frames
docs.text:
Each WebSocket message travels as one or more frames:

 byte 0            byte 1                   then                       then           then
+-----+--------+------+-------------+  +-------------------------+  +-----------+  +---------+
| FIN | opcode | MASK | length (7b) |  | 2 or 8 more length bytes|  | 4-byte    |  | payload |
| 1b  | 4b     | 1b   |             |  | if length is 126 or 127 |  | mask key  |  |         |
+-----+--------+------+-------------+  +-------------------------+  +-----------+  +---------+
  • FIN marks the last frame of a message; opcode says what it is: 1 text, 2 binary, 8 close, 9 ping, 10 pong (0 continues a split message).
  • The 7-bit length holds the payload length directly up to 125. The value 126 means "the real length is in the next 2 bytes", 127 "in the next 8 bytes" (big-endian). A 300-byte masked console message therefore starts 81 FE 01 2C: final text frame, mask bit plus 126, then the 16-bit length 300.
  • The MASK bit and the 4-byte mask key are present on frames from the client.

ws::decode returns Ok(None) when the buffer does not yet hold a whole frame, and the number of bytes it used when it does, so the connection loop can drain exactly one frame and keep any bytes of the next:

// src/remote/server.rs, the connection loop (simplified)
loop {
    let (frame, used) = match ws::decode(&buf) {
        Ok(Some(f)) => f,
        Ok(None) => break,        // wait for more bytes from the socket
        Err(_) => break 'conn,    // protocol violation: drop the connection
    };
    buf.drain(..used);
    // … handle frame.opcode and frame.payload
}

docs.title: Masking: why every browser frame is XORed
docs.text:
Every frame a browser sends is masked: the browser picks 4 random bytes per frame and XORs payload byte i with mask byte i % 4. Masking is not encryption — the key is sent right in front of the payload. Its purpose is to protect proxies and caches in the network path. A malicious page could otherwise choose payload bytes that look like an HTTP request to a confused intermediary and poison its cache; with a random mask chosen by the browser, the page cannot control the bytes that appear on the wire.

So the rules are asymmetric:

Direction Masked? What OpenInterceptor does Client → server Always (RFC 6455 §5.3) ws::decode refuses an unmasked frame as an error ("client frames must be masked") and unmasks the payload Server → client Never ws::encode writes the plain payload

Unmasking is one line, because XOR undoes itself ((b ^ m) ^ m == b):

// src/remote/ws.rs, decode
let mask = [buf[at], buf[at + 1], buf[at + 2], buf[at + 3]];
at += 4;
let payload = buf[at..at + len].iter().enumerate().map(|(i, b)| b ^ mask[i % 4]).collect();

RFC 6455 §5.7 has a worked example: the masked text frame "Hello" is

81 85 37 FA 21 3D 7F 9F 4D 51 58
│  │  └─ mask ──┘ └─ "Hello" XOR mask ┘
│  └ MASK bit set, length 5
└ FIN + opcode 1 (text)

and remote::ws::frames_decode_masked_wait_for_more_bytes_and_encode decodes exactly those bytes. The server's unmasked reply of the same message is just 81 05 48 65 6C 6C 6F.

tools/console_client.py (Python standard library) does the client's side by hand — random key, handshake, masked frames — which makes it a second, independent implementation to test the server against.

docs.title: Defensive limits
docs.text:
A server on a network must assume its peer may be broken or hostile. The console server:

  • refuses a request head over 16 KB and a frame over 64 KB (http::MAX_HEAD, ws::MAX_FRAME) before allocating for it, so a bogus 8-byte length cannot make it reserve gigabytes;
  • rejects nesting deeper than 32 levels in JSON, so [[[[… cannot overflow the stack of the recursive-descent parser;
  • serves only peers on the local network (server::is_local) and acts only after the pairing code.

docs.title: Threads and channels in Rust
docs.text:
The game loop must never wait for the network, so the server runs on its own threads and the game talks to them through channels (std::sync::mpsc). A channel has a Sender and a Receiver; each end can be moved to another thread, and values sent through it change owner, so no data is shared and nothing needs a lock:

let (tx, events) = std::sync::mpsc::channel();      // tx: Sender<Event>, events: Receiver<Event>
std::thread::spawn(move || accept_loop(listener, code, tx, clients, stop));  // tx moves in
// … later, once per frame on the game thread:
let new_events: Vec<Event> = events.try_iter().collect();   // never blocks

The one piece of state both sides need — the list of connected clients — is an Arc<Mutex<Vec<Client>>>: Arc (atomically reference-counted) lets several threads own it, and Mutex lets one at a time change it. Simple flags such as "this client has paired" and "stop accepting" are Arc<AtomicBool>, which needs no lock at all. The compiler enforces this: a type that is not safe to send between threads (an Rc, a RefCell) cannot be moved into thread::spawn, so the mistakes that cause data races elsewhere do not compile.
