docs.title: Mod designer, cutscene designer and game bundling
docs.text:
Status: planned, not built; decisions D1–D5 made by the user on 2026-11-11

This design is normative for the requirements that cite it. The five choices of the proposal were answered by the user on 2026-11-11 (Decisions): D1 and D2 accepted (with the Linux video path recorded), D3 yes, D4 accepted with a further harmless flag, and D5 a separate designer program in the same repository. The Linux video path still needs its dependency evaluation before it is built. Further decisions of 2026-11-11 added 3D cockpit instrument placement, the first test case (an X-COM 3D cockpit), single-file models and the name extension (sections 2.1 – 2.5).

Features: F-MOD-009 – F-MOD-015, F-PLT-005. Requirements: R-MOD-021 – R-MOD-055, R-PLT-007 – R-PLT-010. Plan: MD1 in Stage 4, MD2 – MD3 in Stage 6, MD4 – MD6 and MD8 – MD10 in Stage 7, MD7 in Stage 8 (where it goes).

A companion Mod Designer application lets a player build packs and mods without editing files by hand:

  • A new pack starts from a chosen base.
  • Any asset of the parent can be imported for editing. The model, its materials and textures are copied together and edited in an external program such as Blender; the designer reloads them live.
  • A Cutscene Designer inside it builds introduction films and story scenes with the game engine itself. It provides:
    • a timeline of keyframed scripted entities and AI-driven autopilot entities;
    • formations, weapons fire and timed destruction;
    • timed sounds;
    • fixed or attached cameras, with camera cuts;
    • a 3D map of the whole scene and a live preview of the current frame.
  • Any cutscene can instead be a video file.
  • The build system gains product bundling: a creator can ship a complete game, engine plus chosen packs, branded as their own, without players installing anything by hand.

Everything the designer writes is the same open YAML, OBJ, PNG and WAV data the engine already reads, so nothing it makes is locked to the tool.

Source: the user's request, 2026-11-11

"Add to the longer term plan a companion app for a mod designer, which allows a user to define custom packs and mods to add to the game. On creation of a new pack or mod, user may choose a base to use for assets that they are going to override. When editing a mod, they can choose to import an asset from the parent. This duplicates the original asset and its dependencies (model plus textures in most cases) which the user can then edit in an external program, usually blender. A cutscene designer is also needed in the mod tool for users to add introduction film and custom animations that play for key campaign events or at the start of specific mission definitions. The designer can import any assets into the cut scene. For fighters and ships, they can choose which formation to apply. Cutscenes always use basic physics so that the animation behavior is predictable. There are both scripted entities and autopilot in the cut scenes - autopilot will run based on beginner AI rules given designated targets and usually serve as background action. Scripted entities can be keyframed, allowing motion to be defined along with weapons fire and time triggered destruction. So this requires the ability to add and remove objects from the scene at specific times, move them in 3d space, set keyframes for position, rotation, speed (speed overridden when keyframe positions are set to guarantee that the positioning is correct), and assign targets for them to chase, capture, or shoot at. Sounds must be included at timed positions so that narration, music, and other audio can be played. Cameras can be defined at explicit positions or attached to an object. If attached, then the camera's coordinates are set relative to the parent object and positioning is keyframed for distance and orbit. User needs to be able to see the overall 3d map and preview of the current animation frame. Switching between cameras in the cutscene is set through keyframes. Produce a design PDF for the modding and animation features. Note that a user may also provide a video to play instead of scripted engine animation. Build system needs to accommodate bundling specific mods/packs into the distributable or application bundle so that users can release a complete game without requiring manual download and installation of packs and mods to their local folders."

With decision D4 the user added: "Also a flag for the animations for their weapons to cause no damage."

Source: the user's message of 2026-11-11 (3D cockpits, extensions, packs and mods)

"for xcom cockpits, we will be designing a 3d cockpit in blender to include as an example mod that substitutes the 3d to replace the 2d image. This raises a point for the mod design tools, they need to accommodate placement of the UI elements so that they are projected onto the correct faces in a 3d view. Simple handling will be to allow each element to be dragged around the screen to detemine their positions and then previewed by applying to the geometry that it is over. this will be the first test case for the mod design tools when available - a mod extending interceptor, where user selects the cockpit images to extract, they are copied into the mod, select to create a 3d cockpit (which will provide a generic base cockpit geometry defined in default if none is present in the parent). The user can then edit it in Blender. If possible, it would be ideal to allow the .blend files to be included in addtition to standaole mtl and obj objects so that a user can package the object, material, and textures into a single file, but that is not strictly necessary as long as the correct relationshps between materials and their texture images is consistently maintained.

Open points Hit static - correct, works well now Let's call it an extension as opposed to an override, since another pack is the base and we are either adding to or overriding assets. Will have to consider where the distinction is between pack and mod in that case, but conceptually packs are "baked into" the game on build where mods are added externally in user's local files."

On the single-file plan (section 2.5): "ok that works. obj/mtl as in the existing packs of course would continue to be supported."

docs.title: 1. Goals and principles
docs.text:
• The files stay the source of truth. The designer is a convenience over the documented pack format.
    • Everything it saves can be read, diffed and hand-edited.
    • Everything hand-written opens in it.
    • It validates with the engine's own --check.
  • One engine. The previews are drawn by the game's renderer and simulated by the game's sim, so what the designer shows is what the game plays.
  • Original content stays private.
    • Importing an asset from the X-COM data converts it into the user's own mod folder, for personal use only.
    • A pack holding converted original assets is marked as such and can never be bundled for release (section 5).
  • Deterministic cutscenes. A cutscene plays the same way every time: fixed tick, seeded randomness, Simple physics.
  • Modest dependencies. No new dependency without the evaluation the project requires; decisions D1 and D2 add none.

docs.title: 2.1 Packs and mods
docs.text:
Action What it does New pack / mod Asks for an id, a name and a kind: campaign (a new game), addon (adds to a campaign) or extension (another pack is the base; it adds to or overrides that pack's assets). Asks for a base: the default campaign (resources/default), interceptor, or any installed pack. Writes pack.yaml with parent: and creates the folder skeleton (rules/, models/, textures/, sounds/, text/en/, missions/, scenarios/, cutscenes/). Open / edit A pack tree, with definitions grouped as ships, weapons, missions, cutscenes, text and so on. A form editor generated from the engine's schemas — the same ones that produce the JSON Schemas — so new keys appear without designer changes. A raw YAML view. Import from parent Pick any asset the parent provides: a model, texture, sound, image or cockpit. The designer copies it and its dependencies into the mod at the path that overrides the original (2.2). Original formats (XMSH, XTXR, TGA, ADPCM WAV) are converted to OBJ/MTL, PNG and WAV by the extractor that already exists. Edit externally "Open in Blender" (or any program set per file type) launches the external editor on the copied file. A file watcher reloads the asset in the preview on save, using the engine's model cache. Validate and play The engine validator runs on every save; each problem is reported with its file, line and key. "Play" starts the testbed with the mod enabled, on a chosen scenario or mission. Package Exports the pack as a folder or zip for sharing, or adds it to a product bundle (section 5).

Decided (2026-11-11): extension, not override

The user: "Let's call it an extension as opposed to an override, since another pack is the base and we are either adding to or overriding assets." An extension declares parent: and adds to or overrides the base's assets.

Open

The pack manifest's kinds today are campaign, addon and library (R-MOD-001). Whether extension becomes a manifest kind of its own or maps onto addon is decided when MD4 is built.

Packs and mods. The same format; the difference is where they come from and whether a build includes them. Packs are "baked into" the game on build: resources/ and the bundled packs/, included in a product bundle (section 5). Mods are added externally, in the user's local mods folder. Open: where exactly the line falls — for example, whether a mod promoted into a product bundle becomes a pack — is to be settled.

docs.title: 2.2 What "an asset and its dependencies" means
docs.text:
Imported Copied with it Ship or object Its definition (the rules entry, with inheritance resolved or kept, at the user's choice); its model set (intact, damage-level and construction-state meshes, LODs and overlays); debris pieces and the destroyed effect; each model's materials and textures; its engine and weapon sounds; its text keys. Model The OBJ, its MTL, every texture the MTL names, and its LOD files. Cockpit The cockpit image or 3D model, its instrument layout, and the textures the 3D model uses. Mission or scenario The definition and its text keys. The ships it uses stay references; importing them is offered as a separate choice.

A dependency graph built from the loaded content drives this. The same graph powers "where is this used?" and warns before deleting anything still referenced.

docs.title: 2.3 Instruments on a 3D cockpit
docs.text:
A 3D cockpit's instruments (radar, MFD, gauges, status, message, power, systems…) are drawn on the model's surface at anchors, {at, normal, size} (Cockpits). In the designer:

  1. The modder drags an instrument around the screen over the cockpit model.
  2. On every frame of the drag, a ray from the eye through the cursor is intersected with the model's triangles; the nearest hit gives the anchor's at, and the hit face's normal its normal.
  3. The instrument is previewed applied to that face, drawn by the game's own anchored-instrument path, so it looks as it will in the game. Over no face, it keeps its last anchor.
  4. Its size on the surface is adjustable. Dropping keeps the anchor; saving writes cockpits.<id>.anchors to the mod's rules.

An instrument with only a 2D rectangle gains an anchor the same way; its rectangle still serves the other views.

Reuse. The engine already has the pieces: hud::layout::cursor_ray (the ray through the cursor), hud::layout::ray_triangle (the hit) and hud::layout::anchor_corners (the instrument's rectangle on the surface); the cockpits.<id>.anchors key; and the game's F12 layout editor (app/flight.rs, edit_layout), which drags 2D rectangles and already places an existing anchor where the dashboard is clicked. The designer reuses them. As a first step, the F12 editor could gain the drag with live preview, and anchors for instruments that have none.

Requirements: R-MOD-048, R-MOD-049.

docs.title: 2.4 First test case: an X-COM 3D cockpit
docs.text:
The first test case for the mod tools, when they are available, is a mod that extends interceptor with a 3D X-COM cockpit:

  1. The modder selects the cockpit images to extract. They are copied into the mod — converted from the original data by the extractor, with their provenance recorded, for personal use only and never bundled.
  2. Create 3D cockpit copies the parent's cockpit model into the mod or, when the parent has none, a generic base cockpit defined in resources/default: an original-free OBJ/MTL model with its textures, generated by tools/default_assets/, with dashboard surfaces and default anchors for the standard instruments.
  3. The modder edits the model in Blender (live reload, 2.1).
  4. The modder places the instruments on it (2.3).

Separately, the user intends to design an X-COM 3D cockpit in Blender and ship it as an example mod in packs/ that replaces the 2D cockpit image with a 3D one. Its geometry is original-free; the X-COM cockpit textures are referenced from the player's original data, not copied, and the mod declares requires_original: true. Open: an MTL names its textures by file path, so how the model refers to a texture in the original data is settled with MD9.

Requirements: R-MOD-050, R-MOD-051, R-MOD-052.

docs.title: 2.5 Single-file models and Blender sources
docs.text:
• OBJ/MTL stays. Wavefront OBJ/MTL with separate texture files remains a fully supported format: it is what the existing packs use, and nothing below replaces it.
  • .glb as an additional option. Binary glTF is one file holding mesh, materials and textures. Blender exports it natively, and the engine can read it in-crate: a JSON chunk (the crate already has a JSON parser, src/remote/json.rs) and binary buffers. No dependency.
  • .blend as the source only. A mod may carry its .blend files. When Blender is installed, the designer runs it headless on save to export OBJ/MTL or .glb (blender -b file.blend --python-expr …). The engine never parses .blend, whose binary format changes between Blender versions. Blender is an optional external tool, not a dependency (Dependency policy).
  • Materials keep their textures. On every import and export, each material stays with its texture images: MTL map_Kd paths are relative to the .mtl file and inside the pack.

The user called single files "not strictly necessary as long as the correct relationshps between materials and their texture images is consistently maintained", and confirmed this plan: "ok that works. obj/mtl as in the existing packs of course would continue to be supported."

Requirements: R-MOD-053, R-MOD-054, R-MOD-055.

docs.title: 3. The Cutscene Designer
docs.text: A cutscene is a short film played by the engine at a campaign event, at the start of a specific mission, or as the campaign's introduction. The designer edits it on a timeline, previews it frame by frame, and saves it as cutscenes/<id>.yaml in the pack.

docs.title: 3.1 Layout
docs.text:
┌──────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
│ Scene            │ 3D map (whole scene)          │ Preview (active camera, t)    │
│ ▸ Entities       │                               │                               │
│   lightning_1    │   paths · keyframes ·         │   engine renderer,            │
│   lightning_2    │   camera frusta               │   current frame               │
│   wraith_* ×4    │                               │                               │
│   xcom_base      │                               │                               │
│ ▸ Cameras        │                               │                               │
│ ▸ Sounds         │                               │                               │
│ ▸ Captions       │                               │                               │
├──────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┤
│ Timeline  ▶ 00:12.40                                                             │
│ lightning_1 pos   ◆──────◆────────◆                                              │
│ lightning_1 fire          ●                                                      │
│ camera cut        ▮            ▮                                                 │
│ narration           ▭▭▭▭▭▭▭▭                                                     │
│ wraith_3 destroy                ✕                                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

The outline of the scene (left), the 3D map of the whole scene with paths and camera frusta (centre), the preview through the active camera at the current frame (right), and the timeline with tracks, keyframes and the playhead (bottom). An inspector panel for the selection opens on the right.

docs.title: 3.2 What a scene contains
docs.text: Element Behaviour Scripted entity Any ship, object or debris from the loaded packs. It has enter and leave times, and keyframes for position, rotation and speed. When position keyframes exist, the speed is derived from the path (overriding speed keys), so the entity is exactly where the keyframes say at each time. It has actions at times: fire beams or a missile at a target, start chasing a target, capture a target with the tractor, be destroyed (with its looks and debris), jump to hyperspace. A harmless flag, on the entity or on one action, makes its weapons fire and show their effects but deal no damage (D4). Autopilot entity Flown by the engine's AI with the beginner difficulty rules, so it is predictable. It is given designated targets (attack, escort, flee to a point), usually as background action. An optional per-entity aggressive flag livens up background dogfights, and harmless works as for a scripted entity (D4). It may be switched to scripted at a time, and back. Formation A group of fighters or ships placed by a named formation (vee, line abreast, echelon, box, diamond, or a custom one). It has a leader, which is scripted or autopilot. Formations are pack data (formations:) shared with wingman flying, so a cutscene and a battle use the same shapes. Sound A clip at a time on a sound track: narration, music or effects. It has a volume and a fade in and out, and is either positioned (attached to an entity) or flat. Music can duck under narration. Caption Optional subtitle text (a text key, so it can be translated) shown over a time range. It makes narration accessible (D3: yes). Camera Fixed: keyframed world position and look target or rotation, plus field of view. Attached: parented to an entity, with keyframed distance, orbit (yaw and pitch around the parent), height and look offset; its coordinates are relative to the parent. Camera cuts A track of keyframes, each choosing the active camera. Each cut is instant or a short blend. Environment Starfield seed, sun, backdrop, and later terrain and atmosphere (Stage 3.3–3.5).

docs.title: 3.3 How it plays: deterministic, with Simple physics
docs.text:
• A cutscene runs on the normal 60 Hz sim with a fixed seed, and every ship flies Simple physics (R-FLT-013). Motion is what the keyframes say, and autopilot traffic is repeatable.
  • Paths: position keyframes are joined by a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline, which passes through every key without overshooting at sharp corners. Rotations use quaternion slerp. A ship with position keys and no rotation keys faces along its path, banking into turns.
  • Scrubbing: the preview seeks by replaying the simulation from the nearest snapshot. Snapshots of the whole world are taken every 2 s while playing, so seeking stays quick and exact.
  • Destruction and fire: these are actions on the timeline that call the same simulation functions as a battle — a beam shot, a missile launch, Destroyed with debris. The same effects and sounds play.

docs.title: 3.4 The cutscene file
docs.text:
id: intro
title: "@cutscene.intro.title"
length: 48s
environment: {starfield_seed: 31, sun: [-0.4, 0.45, -0.8]}
entities:
  lead: {class: lightning, enter: 0s, keys: {position: [[0s, [0,0,0]], [6s, [400,50,-1800]]]},
         actions: [[4.5s, fire_beams, {target: drone_1}]]}
  wing: {formation: vee, leader: lead, class: [lightning, lightning], harmless: true}
  drone_1: {class: wraith, autopilot: {attack: lead}, aggressive: true, harmless: true,
            enter: 2s, leave: 9s, destroy_at: 5.2s}
cameras:
  wide:  {fixed: {keys: {position: [[0s, [0,300,900]]], look_at: [[0s, lead]]}, fov: 55}}
  chase: {attach: lead, keys: {distance: [[0s, 60], [5s, 25]], orbit: [[0s, [0,10]], [5s, [40,5]]]}}
cuts: [[0s, wide], [3.5s, chase, {blend: 0.5s}]]
sounds: [[0s, music/theme.wav, {volume: 0.6, fade_in: 2s, duck: true}],
         [1s, voice/narration_01.wav]]
captions: [[1s, 6s, "@cutscene.intro.line1"]]

Or, for a film made elsewhere: id: intro, video: video/intro.mp4, with optional captions:.

Where cutscenes play:

  • campaign: {intro: intro} — the campaign's introduction;
  • an event action play_cutscene(intro);
  • a mission's intro: <cutscene id>, or outro: {win: …, lose: …}.

A cutscene can always be skipped with Esc, the console's skip button or the pad's Start button.

The key names above are the proposal's; they are fixed, with their schema and the Modding pages, when MD2 is built.

As built (MD2, app 0.13.0)

The format as built is a subset, documented key by key on Modding › Cutscenes: id, title, length, environment {starfield_seed, sun, environment}; entities with class, faction, enter, leave, keys.position, actions ([time, fire_beams, secs], [time, missile, target], [time, destroy]), destroy_at and harmless; cameras fixed (position keys and look_at — an entity or a point — directly on the camera, not under fixed: {keys: …}) or attached (attach, distance and orbit keys directly on the camera, not under keys:), each with fov; cuts (instant); sounds naming the campaign's event sounds ([time, name, volume]); captions as plain text. It plays as the campaign intro (campaign.intro), from events (play_cutscene) and with --cutscene; Esc or Enter skips. Not built: formations, autopilot entities and aggressive, rotation and speed keys, chase/capture/jump actions, harmless on a single action (per entity it works since app 0.14.1), sound files with fades and ducking, text-key captions, blended cuts, mission intros and outros, video: in a cutscene, skipping from the console or pad, scrubbing and snapshots. The original's Smacker films play through campaign.intro_video, video(…) and an ending's video (app 0.12.0 – 0.13.0). DEV-054.

docs.title: 3.5 Video instead of animation
docs.text:
A pack can provide a video file for any cutscene. The engine has no video decoder for modern formats today, and the Smacker decoder planned for 6.3 covers only the original's films. Decision D2: mod videos play through the operating system's own media framework, behind the platform shim, with image sequences plus a WAV track as the fallback that always works:

  • macOS: AVFoundation.
  • Windows: Media Foundation.
  • Linux: GStreamer, when installed, is loaded at run time with dlopen — no crate dependency and no link-time dependency. GStreamer is LGPL; loading the system's own copy dynamically, without bundling it, keeps the project clear of it. Without GStreamer, mod videos fall back to image sequences.

Open

The Linux path (GStreamer through dlopen) must be evaluated on the dependency page — complexity, stability, licence — before it is built (MD3).

docs.title: 4. How the designer is built
docs.text:
• A separate program in the same repository, sharing the engine library (D5). openinterceptor-designer is a second binary in the same crate, using content, sim, render and audio directly. The previews are therefore the real engine, and the designer cannot drift from it. Being its own program keeps its interface focused, and the game and the designer can run side by side. The build produces two artifacts: the game and the designer.
  • Interface (D1). macroquad's built-in immediate-mode UI module for panels, forms and the timeline, with the engine renderer drawing the 3D map and preview viewports. This adds no new dependency. Forms are generated from the schema types (content::schema::Ty), which already describe every key with a help text.
  • Editing model.
    • An in-memory document per open file, with an undo stack of edits.
    • Saving writes YAML through the existing writer and keeps comments where possible. Hand-written files are rewritten only in the keys that changed.
  • Engine additions.
    • cutscene: the file format and validation, plus a player that drives sim and the camera from the timeline.
    • formations: shared pack data.
    • Video playback through the platform layer.
    • The game plays cutscenes at campaign events and before missions.
  • Testing.
    • Unit tests for spline and slerp sampling, keyframe evaluation and the speed override, action timing, snapshot seeking (seek, then play, must equal straight play), dependency-graph import, and YAML round-trips.
    • Manual tests for the designer's interface.

docs.title: 5. Bundling a complete game
docs.text:
A creator should be able to release their campaign as a game in its own right, downloaded and played with nothing to install.

  • A product file, product.yaml in the creator's project, describes the bundle:
    • name, version, bundle id and icon;
    • splash image and the intro cutscene;
    • the packs to include, in load order;
    • the default campaign;
    • whether the testbed, model viewer and developer tools are shown (off for a release);
    • licence and credit files.
  • The build produces two artifacts, the game and the designer (D5). A product bundle is built from the game artifact; the designer stays a separate program.

  • The build tool — tools/build_bundle.py --product product.yaml, or the designer's "Package game":

    • copies the engine, resources/default (if used) and exactly the listed packs into the bundle;
    • names and brands the app;
    • starts it directly in the chosen campaign;
    • writes the macOS .app now, and the Linux and Windows packages when Stage 8 adds them.

    Players' own mods still load from their user folder on top. - Safety: nothing original is ever bundled. The bundler refuses: - a pack with requires_original; - any file marked as converted from original data. The designer records the provenance of imported assets in pack.yaml, and the extractor already knows which files it converted.

    A pack built on interceptor can be shared as a mod for people who own the game, but never bundled into a product. - Validation first. The full validator runs and must report no errors before a bundle is written.

docs.title: 6. Where it goes in the plan
docs.text: Item Scope Stage (design) Placed in MD1 Shared formations: data, used by wingmen first (it also replaces today's per-scenario offsets) Stage 3 / 4 Stage 4; it also serves wingmen MD2 Cutscene format, validation and the in-game player (timeline, spline paths, actions, cameras, cuts, sounds, captions); playing at campaign intro, events and mission intro and outro; skip Stage 6 Stage 6 MD3 Video playback for mod cutscenes via the platform layer (D2; the Linux dlopen path evaluated first) Stage 6 Stage 6 MD4 Designer application shell (a separate program and build artifact, D5; macroquad UI, D1): pack wizard with base selection, pack tree, schema-driven forms and YAML view, validation, play in testbed Stage 7 Stage 7 MD5 Asset import with dependencies (including conversion from original formats), external editor launch, live reload, "where used", provenance recording Stage 7 Stage 7 MD6 Cutscene Designer: outline, 3D map, preview, timeline with keyframes, cameras and cuts, sounds, captions, scrubbing with snapshots Stage 7 Stage 7 MD8 3D cockpit instrument placement: drag each instrument over the cockpit model, ray-cast to the face below the cursor, preview applied to it, adjustable size, saved as anchors Stage 7 Stage 7 MD9 First test case for the mod tools: an interceptor extension with a 3D X-COM cockpit (extract the cockpit images, Create 3D cockpit, edit in Blender, place instruments); the generic base cockpit in resources/default; the X-COM 3D cockpit example mod in packs/ Stage 7 Stage 7 MD10 Single-file models: .glb reader (in-crate) beside OBJ/MTL; .blend sources exported through Blender when installed; materials keep their textures Stage 7 Stage 7 MD7 Product bundling: the build's two artifacts (game and designer, D5); product.yaml, branded builds, release mode without developer tools, the provenance guard Stage 8 Stage 8

docs.title: 7. Decisions
docs.text:
Proposed with recommendations; answered by the user on 2026-11-11.

# Question Decision (2026-11-11) D1 The designer's interface toolkit Accepted: macroquad's built-in UI module plus the engine renderer for the viewports; no new dependency. (The alternative, a local web interface with streamed preview frames, is not taken.) D2 How to play mod videos Accepted: the operating system's media framework through the platform shim — AVFoundation on macOS, Media Foundation on Windows — with image sequences plus WAV as the fallback that always works. Linux: GStreamer, when installed, is loaded at run time with dlopen (no crate dependency, no link-time dependency); GStreamer is LGPL, and loading the system's copy dynamically, without bundling it, keeps the project clear of it; without GStreamer, mod videos fall back to image sequences. Open: the Linux path must be evaluated on the dependency page before it is built. An in-crate MP4/H.264 decoder is out of scope. D3 Captions in cutscenes Yes: captions are text keys, translatable. D4 Autopilot difficulty in cutscenes Accepted: autopilot uses the beginner AI rules, with an optional per-entity aggressive flag. Added by the user: "Also a flag for the animations for their weapons to cause no damage." — a per-entity and per-action harmless flag: its weapons fire and show their effects but deal no damage. D5 Where the designer lives A separate program in the same repository, so its interface stays focused and the game and the designer can run in parallel. The build produces two artifacts: the game and the designer.

docs.title: Format: behaviours and scripting
docs.text: Status: Tier 1 behaviours and conditions (object context) implemented in Stage 2; actions, the battle and campaign contexts, the remaining manoeuvres, targeting preferences and Tier 2 are design. Replaces the open question on Scripting with a two-tier design; the Tier 2 language decision is evaluated (Stage 3.10) and awaits the user. The implemented form is documented for modders on Behaviours and conditions.

docs.title: Two tiers
docs.text:
Tier What Who needs it 1. Declarative Behaviours, missions and events written as YAML definitions, with a small condition and action language for the parts that vary (hull < 0.3, research(plasma), spawn(wave_2)). Implemented in-crate: a lexer, parser, type checker and interpreter of a few hundred lines each — itself a teaching example. Everything. Both shipped campaigns (interceptor, default) are written entirely in Tier 1. 2. Scripts Optional script files for behaviour Tier 1 cannot express (a boss with bespoke phases, a puzzle mission, a procedural campaign generator). Called through named hooks from Tier 1. Mods that want it.

Why not scripts for everything: Tier 1 definitions can be validated before play (every reference and type checked by --check), saved trivially (they are data), run deterministically at the fixed 60 Hz tick, and edited by someone who does not program. The original game's behaviour is hard-coded C++ whose logic is a fixed set of states and parameters, so Tier 1 is a natural fit for it.

docs.title: Conditions
docs.text:
A condition is an expression that evaluates to true or false. The same language is used in every when, requires, visible_when and if key across the format. Implemented for the object context (reference, architecture).

hull < 0.3 and not system_damaged(engines)
research(plasma_beam) and day >= 30
relation(cartel) <= -20 or flag(cartel_betrayed)
count(ships, faction: alien, class: fighter, within: 5km) >= 3
difficulty >= veteran
  • Values: numbers (with units m, km, s, min, h, day, %, converted to base units), booleans, ids as query arguments (plasma_beam), and the difficulty levels as ordered constants. (Implemented: all but strings, which no context needs yet.)
  • Operators: + - * /, comparisons, and or not, parentheses.
  • Functions: a fixed, documented query API per context (below). Unknown names, wrong argument types and misspelt ids are load errors, not run-time surprises.
  • No assignment, no loops, no user functions: a condition cannot change the game and always terminates.
Context Queries available (examples) Object (behaviours) — implemented hull, shields, energy, speed, has_target, target_distance, target_hull, target_disabled, target_is_player, time_in_state, hit_recently(t), random(p), system_damaged(x), threats(d), allies(d), missiles, difficulty, disabled, towing, prize_near(d). Not yet: target_class, ammo(x). Battle (missions) count(...), alive(name), destroyed(name), disabled(name), captured(name), time, objective(x), player_hull, near(a, b, d) Campaign (events, strategy) day, date, money, research(x), researching(x), module(x), owns(system), relation(faction), flag(x), counter(x), missions_won(type), losses(class), resource(x), threat(system), difficulty

random(p) draws from the game's seeded generator, so a replay or reload gives the same result.

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
An action changes the game. Action lists appear in events, mission outcomes and behaviour transitions; they run in order.

spawn(wave_2)
message(@msg.convoy_spotted, from: freighter_1)
set_flag(cartel_betrayed); add(relation(cartel), -30); add(money, 250000)
unlock(research: alien_navigation); start_mission(nova_theft, system: kepler)

The action vocabulary per context is fixed and documented in the reference (Stage 3 and 4 implement it). As with queries, everything is checked at load time.

docs.title: Behaviours: behaviours: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
A behaviour is a state machine for one object: states, each running a built-in manoeuvre with parameters, and transitions with conditions. Built-in manoeuvres cover what the original AI does; their parameters are the tuning.

The implemented form (Stage 2):

behaviours:
  wraith:
    start: engage
    states:                        # state: manoeuvre and its parameters
      engage:
        do: attack
        range: 1.6km
        fire_cone: 3
        burst: {per_level: [0.6s, 0.8s, 1s, 1.2s, 1.5s]}
        pause: {per_level: [2s, 1.6s, 1.2s, 0.9s, 0.6s]}
        missiles: {per_level: [0, 0, 14s, 11s, 8s]}
      jink: {do: evade, duration: 2s}
      flee: {do: retreat, jump: true}
    transitions:                   # tried in order; from "*" = any state
      - {from: engage, to: jink, when: "hit_recently(0.3s) and random(0.4)"}
      - {from: jink, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 2s"}
      - {from: "*", to: flee, when: "hull < 15% and difficulty >= veteran"}
    skill:
      aim: {per_level: [0.2, 0.35, 0.5, 0.65, 0.8]}
      reaction: {per_level: [1.3s, 1s, 0.8s, 0.6s, 0.4s]}
    variants:                      # per difficulty level: only what differs
      beginner: {transitions: [{from: engage, to: jink, when: "random(0.2)"}]}

Still design: targeting preferences (target: {player: 3, wingman: 2, freighter: 1}), more manoeuvre parameters (evade_when_hit, jink, lead, retreat to a point), and wingman orders as transitions. The original design sketch, in today's syntax:

behaviours:
  wraith:
    start: engage
    states:
      engage: {do: attack, range: 1.5km, fire_cone: 8, burst: 2s, evade_when_hit: true}
      evade: {do: evade, duration: 3s, jink: 40}
      flee: {do: retreat, to: nearest_friendly_base}
    transitions:
      - {from: engage, to: evade, when: "hit_recently(1s) and random(0.4)"}
      - {from: evade, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 3s"}
      - {from: "*", to: flee, when: "hull < 25% and difficulty >= veteran"}
    target: {player: 3, wingman: 2, freighter: 1}     # targeting preferences, scored
    skill: {aim: 0.6, reaction: 0.8s}
    variants:
      beginner:
        skill: {aim: 0.35, reaction: 1.4s}
        transitions:                                  # at Beginner they never flee
          - {from: engage, to: evade, when: "hit_recently(1s) and random(0.4)"}
          - {from: evade, to: engage, when: "time_in_state > 3s"}
      superhuman:
        skill: {aim: 0.9, reaction: 0.3s}
        states:
          engage: {range: 2km, fire_cone: 12, burst: 3s, lead: true}

docs.title: Difficulty variants (implemented)
docs.text:
Any definition — not only behaviours — can carry a variants: mapping with an entry per difficulty level, holding only the keys that differ; at that level the entry is merged over the definition (maps merge, lists and values replace). Levels are defined by the campaign ruleset (campaign: {difficulty: [beginner, experienced, veteran, genius, superhuman], default_difficulty: veteran} — the original's five), so a mod can have any number. (The earlier kind:id@level section idea was replaced by variants when the rules moved to YAML.)

A value that varies by difficulty does not need a variant: any number accepts one value per level, starting_money: {per_level: [5000000, 4500000, 4000000, 3500000, 3000000]}, as the original's Think.ini and *Goodies sections do (a shorter list repeats its last value).

docs.title: Built-in manoeuvres
docs.text: Implemented: idle, circle, patrol (circle round the spawn point), attack, evade, retreat (with jump), turret, tow. Design: the rest of this list. idle, patrol (route or area), formation (on a leader), attack (pursuit with firing discipline), strafe (attack runs on large targets), evade, retreat (to a point or hyperspace out), escort (stay near and defend), intercept (cut off a target before it reaches a point), tow (tug: tractor and haul a disabled ship), launch (carrier/freighter launching craft), turret (stationary aim and fire), mine (proximity trigger), probe (station-keeping with sensor/jamming effect), follow_path (convoy), dock. Each manoeuvre's parameters are documented with defaults. Wingmen use the same system with player orders as transitions ({from: "*", to: attack, when: "order(attack_my_target)"}; implemented so far as fixed wingman orders, with the class behaviour's attack parameters and skill).

docs.title: Weapon and equipment behaviours
docs.text: Weapons are behaviours too, with fewer states: a missile class names a guidance behaviour (homing, sidestep, dumbfire, cloaked_wait, decoy, cluster, proximity) with parameters; special equipment (ECM, cloak, tractor, VCT, damage control) names a built-in system with parameters. New combinations are data; new primitives need engine code or a Tier 2 hook.

docs.title: Tier 2: scripts
docs.text:
A Tier 1 definition can hand control to a script through a hook:

behaviours:
  portal_guardian:
    states:
      phase_3: {do: script, call: "scripts/guardian.lua:phase_3", every: 0.5s}

events:
  custom_ending:
    do: ["script(scripts/ending.lua:run)"]
  • Scripts see the same query and action API as Tier 1 (so nothing is reachable from a script that is not documented), run on the simulation tick, and must be deterministic (no clock, no files, no network; random numbers only from the game's generator).
  • Scripts may keep state only through the API (set_flag, counter, object variables), so saves never need to serialise a script VM.

docs.title: Language decision (Stage 3.10) — awaiting the user
docs.text:
The full evaluation is on the dependency page: Tier 2 scripting, evaluated. No decision has been made.

Option Assessment (summary) (a) Lua 5.4 via mlua The modding standard; fast; MIT. Costs: bundled C sources, a C compiler on every platform, an FFI boundary, opt-in sandboxing, determinism care (f64, table iteration order). The fallback if mods need a full general-purpose language. (b) rhai Pure Rust, MIT/Apache; slower; few modders know it; a larger crate tree; errors at run time. Reconsider only if a pure-Rust or WebAssembly build becomes a requirement. (c) Grow Tier 1 into a small statement language (variables, if/else, bounded loops, functions, calls into the same checked API) No dependency; checked at load, deterministic and sandboxed by construction; the parser, checker and evaluator exist. Ceiling: no general-purpose data structures. Recommended as the default by the evaluator.

Earlier drafts of this page recommended (a) and rejected (c) unless both crates failed evaluation; the evaluation found (c) far cheaper than that assumed, because the language's hard parts already exist. The hook syntax above (do: script, script(...)) is the same for any choice; the .lua file names in the examples are placeholders.

Because both shipped campaigns need only Tier 1, the choice can be made on its merits without blocking any campaign work.

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text: Version Date Change 1.0.0 2026-11-11 Adopted into Specification 1.0.0 as a normative format page; requirements link here 1.12.0 2026-11-11 Tier 2 language decision: summary of the recorded evaluation ((a) mlua, (b) rhai, (c) grow Tier 1); evaluator recommends (c), fallback (a); awaiting the user's decision

docs.title: Format: campaign and game flow
docs.text: Status: design, except the difficulty levels (campaign: {difficulty, default_difficulty}), implemented in Stage 2; campaign: and starts: in Stage 4, arcs, plans, score and endings in Stage 5. The campaign ruleset is the top of a campaign mod: it says how a game starts, how time runs, which systems are switched on, how difficulty scales it, how it is scored and how it ends. Story progression is expressed with events and arcs (below); everything else is in the strategy rules.

docs.title: campaign:
docs.text:
# campaign/campaign.yaml (interceptor)
campaign:
  name: "X-COM: Interceptor"               # implemented (later a text key: "@campaign.name")
  difficulty: [beginner, experienced, veteran, genius, superhuman]   # implemented
  default_difficulty: veteran                                        # implemented
  # --- design (Stages 4 and 5) ---
  player: xcom                         # the player's faction
  start_date: 2067-01-01
  time_speeds: [5s, 1min, 5min, 30min, 1h, 24h]   # game time per real second, one per button
  pause: "event_priority >= high"      # auto-pause condition (see Reports)
  map: frontier                        # a generated or fixed star map
  start: interceptor                   # initial assets
  max_craft_per_mission: 5
  systems: [bases, research, manufacture, purchase, sell, pilots, probes, funding, salvage, capture]
  victory: "flag(doomsday_destroyed)"
  defeat:
    - {when: "flag(doomsday_complete)", ending: "@end.doomsday"}
    - {when: "count_bases(xcom) == 0", ending: "@end.last_base"}
    - {when: "flag(final_mission_failed)", ending: "@end.final_failed"}
  score: interceptor
  reports: [weekly, monthly]
  music: interceptor
  encyclopaedia: interceptor
Key Meaning player The faction the player commands. start_date, time_speeds, pause Calendar and the time-compression buttons; pause is a condition on events and messages. map A maps: definition: fixed or generated (strategy). start A starts: definition: bases, outposts, ships, pilots, stock, money, known research, relations. difficulty, default_difficulty Ordered level ids (any number) and the level a new game starts at. Implemented: every number in the mod may then be {per_level: [..]}, and any definition may have variants: {<level>: {…}} (behaviours). max_craft_per_mission Ships the player may launch on one mission. systems Strategy features in use. A campaign that omits research simply has no research screen; the default campaign uses them all, a pure dogfight campaign none. victory, defeat Conditions checked after every event and battle; the text key names the ending shown. victory may also be a list, each with its own ending (partial victories). score Score rules (below). reports Periodic reports. music, encyclopaedia Music sets and the in-game encyclopaedia (interface).

docs.title: Start state: starts: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
starts:
  interceptor:
    money: {per_level: [5000000, 4750000, 4500000, 3750000, 3000000]}
    bases: [{template: xcom_start, near: map_start}]
    outposts: {count: 3, near: base_1, faction: corporate}
    ships: {base_1: [lightning, lightning, lightning]}
    pilots: {base_1: {random: 5}}
    stock: {base_1: {sensor_probe: 5, xwinder: 10}}
    research_known: [laser_cannon, xwinder, conversion_drive]   # topics already complete
    rival: {bases: {count: 2, min_distance: 1pc}, outposts: 6, faction: alien}
    flags: []

A base template (base_templates: {xcom_start: …}) lists its modules by slot. near/distance place things on a generated map; a fixed map names systems instead.

docs.title: Arcs: story progression
docs.text:
As built (app 0.10.0 – 0.10.3)

Arcs, plans and endings are built as a simpler subset of this page: arcs.<id>.steps; plans.<id> with owner, stages ({name, count}), start_when, every, chance, raid, warnings (a list of {at, do}) and complete; endings.<id> with text and victory, and campaign_end lists of {when, ending}. Not built: plan budget, ship_visibility (the shipment chance stands in), grant_if_missed, plan_stage(x); endings' image, video, music and continue; reports. Keys: Story layer; differences: DEV-051.

The original's story is a gated chain: each step needs a date, earlier steps and campaign state, and opens the next activity. An arc expresses exactly that, and its steps are events:

arcs:
  doomsday:
    steps:
      - alien_message_1
      - alien_message_2
      - alien_message_3
      - alien_message_4
      - alien_message_5
      - summon_macarthur
      - final_mission

Each step fires once, only after the previous one, when its own when condition holds (dates, research, captures, chances per battle). The arc's state is visible to conditions (arc(doomsday) >= 3), so missions, the rival's plan and reports can depend on story progress. A campaign may have several arcs running in parallel (the default campaign has one main arc and side arcs for third parties).

docs.title: Rival plans: plans: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
The original's opponent pursues a project — the Doomsday device — built from components that must be shipped, which the player can intercept, and whose completion loses the game. The default campaign's villain has a plan of the same shape. A plan is a project with stages, costs, shipments and consequences:

plans:
  doomsday:
    owner: alien
    budget: think:financial/doomsday            # share of the owner's income (strategy rules)
    stages:
      - {component: structural, count: {per_level: [8, 9, 10, 7, 7]}, cost: 100000, ship: doomsday_freighter}
      - {component: weapon, count: {per_level: [8, 8, 8, 7, 6]}}
      - {component: drive, count: {per_level: [9, 8, 7, 6, 5]}}
    start_when: "arc(doomsday) >= 1"
    ship_visibility: {per_level: [65%, 60%, 55%, 50%, 45%]}   # chance a convoy passes within player sensors
    grant_if_missed: [structural, weapon]       # only at beginner, experienced, veteran (variants)
    complete: set_flag(doomsday_complete)
    warnings: {33%: dd_warning_1, 66%: dd_warning_2, 90%: dd_warning_3}

Conditions can read plan progress (plan(doomsday) as a fraction, plan_stage(doomsday)), so missions and events can trigger on how far the rival's development has gone — which is exactly what the default campaign's serial chapters need.

docs.title: Score: scores: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
scores:
  interceptor:
    events:
      alien_base_destroyed: 4500
      alien_outpost_destroyed: 2250
      outpost_defended: 2250
      base_lost: -5000
      refused_outpost_defence: -1500
      kill_fighter: [75, 200]          # by class rank
      salvage_item: item               # per item: the item's score key
    ratings: {phenomenal: 75000, excellent: 50000, very_good: 35000, good: 15000, ok: 0}
    feeds: funding                     # what the score drives (strategy rules)

Score events are named, so each original MissionScores index becomes a named entry (the index-to-meaning mapping is recovered in Stage 4 from the guide's table and play-testing).

docs.title: Reports: reports: {<id>: …}
docs.text: Periodic summaries (weekly news and advice, the monthly evaluation with funding changes) are reports: a period, the evaluation they run (strategy rules), and a text template with {variables} and conditional lines. News items are events with do: "news(@news.id)".

docs.title: Endings
docs.text: endings: {<id>: …}: text, image or video, music, and whether the game can continue (continue: false for defeats). Victory conditions name endings; the original has total and partial victory and three defeats.

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text: Version Date Change 1.0.0 2026-11-11 Adopted into Specification 1.0.0 as a normative format page; requirements link here 1.15.0 2026-11-11 As-built note (app 0.10.0 – 0.10.3): arcs, plans and endings as built, and what of this design is not; the format itself unchanged

docs.title: Format: interface, text and media
docs.text: Status: design; implemented in Stage 6 (screens, skins, media) with the screens' logic in Stage 4; screen sets are specified for 6.9. Files in interface/*.yaml (YAML, like every mod file), text/<language>/, images/, music/, video/.

docs.title: Screens
docs.text:
The engine provides the strategy screens as functional components — the logic and the widgets — and a mod lays them out and skins them. The set follows the original's structure, which is the foundation for every campaign:

Screen id Function Original starmap Interactive map: zoom map/system/object, sensor ranges, time controls, object info and squadron reports, launch probe, launch mission, event prompts CSD (Combat Strategic Display) bases Base list, 3D base view with slots, add/dismantle modules, build/dismantle bases, status overlays (normal, defences, damage) Bases research Topics, current work, progress, rate, estimated completion, blocked capacity Research hangar Equip ship: slots and items, stock designs, assign pilots Equip Ship market Purchase (and selling, recruiting): categories, items with size, cost, stores and quantity, cargo and hangar space, deliveries and escorts Purchase equipment/ships factory Manufacture: items, queue with priorities, progress, capacity Manufacturing pilots Roster in portrait sockets, stats, assignment to ships, training, medical, sack Pilots (Assign Pilots) reports Periodic reports, finances, activity, holdings Status Reports relations Factions, standings and stances, history (campaigns with dynamic relations) — encyclopaedia Categories and entries; unlocked by research and encounters UFOpedia messages Message log, news ticker, event choices Communications, Hypernews briefing, debriefing Mission text, formation grid, forces; recovery, items, score, rating Briefing / Mission debriefing simulator Combat simulator setup Combat Simulator options Keyboard configuration, audio, graphics, the layout switch Options chapter Title card and recap between story chapters (default campaign) — main_menu, load_save, difficulty, credits, ending Shell screens same (title screens) Dialogs — orders The selected squadron's ships and status; Attack, Select new destination, Return to base, Return to base (5 secs) Interceptor Orders launch Docked ships, select up to the launch limit, launch or cancel Launch Mission notice, transmission A campaign notice; a story message with its film, OK, OK (5 secs), allocate new research Alien Transmission choice An event's choices, or fly / decline an offered mission —

A campaign's campaign: {systems: […]} decides which screens are reachable; a mod can add custom panels to a screen (text, gauges and lists bound to campaign queries) and, since Specification 1.19.0, custom screens of its own (R-UI-039).

Specified in 1.19.0 (planned, plan item 6.9)

factory split from market; options and the dialogs orders, launch, notice, transmission and choice added to the table. The requirements are Strategy interface (R-UI-001 – R-UI-040).

docs.title: Layout and skin: screens: {<id>: …}, skins: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
skins:
  deco:                               # default campaign
    fonts:
      title: {image: fonts/poster.png, size: 32}   # bitmap font sheet (or TTF, Stage 5 decision)
      body: {image: fonts/typewriter.png}
    panel: {image: images/ui/panel_chrome.png, slice: 24}        # nine-slice frame
    button: {image: images/ui/button_bakelite.png, slice: 12, hover: images/ui/button_hover.png}
    colours: {text: [0.95, 0.9, 0.75], accent: [0.85, 0.15, 0.1]}
    sounds: {click: sounds/ui/click.wav}

screens:
  starmap:
    skin: deco
    design: [1920, 1080]              # design space, scaled to the window (the cockpit rule)
    background: images/ui/starmap_frame.png
    widgets:
      map: [40, 80, 1400, 940]
      time: [1480, 80, 400, 90]
      info: [1480, 200, 400, 500]
      buttons: {rect: [1480, 740, 400, 280], buttons: [launch_mission, launch_probe, bases, research]}

The interceptor campaign's skin uses the original's wrapper art (WrappersDLL.dll images) by original: reference, laid out like the original screens at 640×480; the remastered mod can supply a widescreen layout.

As built (app 0.11.1)

Skins only, simpler than above: skins.<id> with colours (seven roles: background, panel, border, text, dim, accent, highlight), one panel: {image, slice} and one font (a TrueType file, not a bitmap sheet); campaign.skin chooses it. The launcher and the strategy screen draw through it, and the chapter title card exists as the card(…) story action. Not built: screens: layouts and design spaces, widgets, button, skin sounds, several fonts, custom panels, the other screens; interceptor has a palette-only skin, its wrapper layouts not mapped. Modding › Skins.

As built (app 0.16.0): the testbed layout

screens.starmap: {design, background, widgets: {<name>: [x, y, w, h]}} moves the five engine-placed widgets of the single-grid strategy screen (top, map, nav, info, panel, 1280 × 720 by default), stretched to the window. Since 1.19.0 this is the testbed layout (Two layouts); Modding › Screen layouts.

docs.title: Screen sets: screens: and widgets:
docs.text:
New in Specification 1.19.0 — planned (plan item 6.9)

Everything in this section is specified ahead of the code (R-UI-001 – R-UI-040). Nothing here is built yet. Where it conflicts with the sketch above, this section wins.

A screen set is a campaign's interface: full screens and dialogs, each with its own design space, a background and widgets placed by rectangle, linked by actions. The engine owns what each screen does (its function in the Screens table); the set owns where everything is and what it looks like. A set may define only some screens: the rest open the engine's built-in version (R-UI-019).

Campaign keys

campaign:
  interface:
    layout: screens          # screens (the default when the campaign has a screen set) | testbed
    home: starmap            # the screen `home` returns to
    scale: fit               # fit (default) | integer | stretch — for every screen of the set
    filter: nearest          # nearest (pixel art) | linear
    outside: {colour: [0, 0, 0]}   # the bands around a fitted screen: a colour or {image: …}

Screen keys — screens.<id>

Key Type Meaning design [w, h] The design space every rectangle is written in. interceptor: [640, 480]. background image Drawn over the whole design space first. skin skin id Fonts, colours, frames and sounds for this screen (else the campaign's). dialog bool A dialog, drawn over the screen beneath (Dialogs). clock runs | paused Whether the campaign clock runs while it is shown. Default: runs for starmap, paused otherwise. music state A music state to play while shown (optional). function screen id For a custom screen: whose values, lists and commands it uses (optional). focus list of widget names The keyboard and pad focus order (optional; else spatial). aspects list Alternative layouts by window aspect: {min_aspect, design, widgets} (optional). widgets map <name>: {type, rect, …} — drawn in the order written.

A screen id from the Screens table binds to that engine function; any other id is a custom screen (R-UI-039).

docs.title: Widgets
docs.text:
Every widget has type and rect: [x, y, w, h]; all may have visible and enabled (conditions, Format: behaviours and scripting), tooltip (a text key) and sound. Images are any asset reference — a pack file, or original:<file>#<id> with an optional part @[x, y, w, h].

type Keys Draws / does button images: {up, down, hover, disabled} or text; action; key; repeat A push button; missing states fall back to up (R-UI-006). toggle images: {off, on, hover, disabled}; bind; group, value, default An on/off switch; toggles sharing a group are a radio group bound to one state. label text; font, colour, align A fixed text key. value bind or query; format; font, colour, align A bound value (Bound values and lists). list source; columns: [{bind, width, align, header, font, colour}]; row_height; scroll: {up, down} or scroll_bar; select; activate; quantity: {up, down}; layout: rows \| carousel; empty A scrolling, selectable list; a carousel is a dial of one row at a time. map shape: rect \| round; mask; hover: <widget>; zoom The star map, with a hover box naming object, class and owner. minimap map: <widget> The whole map with the view marked; a click centres. globe image or animation A picture or animation that carries lamp widgets. lamp images: {off, on, blink}; bind (an alert) or when (a condition) A status lamp. clock font or digits: <image strip>; show: [date, time] The campaign date and time. model_view subject: craft \| base \| item \| entry; rotate: {left, right, up, down}; zoom; overlay: <group>; slots: true A 3D view; on bases, slot picking and the overlays. text text or bind; font, colour, align, line_spacing; scroll: {up, down} Wrapped, scrolling text with {variables}. image image or bind A fixed or bound picture. frame image (with slice for nine-slice) A panel behind other widgets. portraits source; ring: {centre, radius, count, start} or grid: [cols, rows] or points; empty; select; page: {previous, next} Sockets of portraits (pilots). grid_view cells: [cols, rows]; icons: {player, hostile, neutral, objective, waypoint} The briefing's formation grid. video — Where a dialog plays its film or face (transmission).

docs.title: Actions
docs.text:
A button's action (or a list's activate) is one action or a list run in order.

Action Does open(<screen>) Show a full screen; the one left is remembered. back Return to the screen left. home Go to campaign.interface.home. dialog(<id>) / close Open a dialog over this screen / close the topmost dialog. speed(<n>) / pause Set the campaign clock's speed (the campaign's speed steps, 1-based) / pause it. run_for(<duration>) Run the clock for that long, then pause (run_for(5s) — the original's "(5 secs)" buttons, derived). <command> A command of the screen's function — e.g. attack, set_destination, return_to_base (orders); buy, sell (market); assign_pilot (pilots); launch (launch); research (transmission). Each screen's commands are listed on the modding site. layout(testbed) Switch to the testbed layout (Two layouts).

docs.title: Bound values and lists
docs.text:
bind names an engine value: the set-wide ones — money, date, time, speed, score, month_score, base.name, base.count, selected.name, selected.class, selected.owner, selected.summary, alert.<name> — and each screen's own (for example order.cargo_used, order.cargo_free, order.hangar_free on market; pilot.<stat> on pilots). query is a campaign query in the condition language (query: "plan(eclipse)"). format is a text key holding {value}.

A list's source names one of its screen's lists (market: items; pilots: roster, docked; launch: docked; orders: ships; …); columns[].bind names the row's fields (items: name, size, cost, stores, quantity, picture, info). Names are checked at load (R-UI-017).

docs.title: Dialogs
docs.text: A screen with dialog: true is drawn over the screen beneath: rect places it in the beneath screen's design space (or design gives it its own space, centred), frame draws its panel and dim darkens the screen beneath (0 – 1). It is modal and dialogs stack. The engine raises orders, launch, notice, transmission and choice itself; one the set does not define falls back to the skin's built-in prompt.

docs.title: Focus and keys
docs.text: Arrows, the d-pad and the left stick move the focus to the nearest enabled widget in that direction (or along focus); Tab / Shift+Tab and the shoulder buttons cycle it; Enter / A activates; Esc / B is close on a dialog and back on a screen. These are interface actions in the controls' action table, so they can be rebound. A widget's key is a hotkey that works whatever has the focus. The skin's focus image (else an outline in highlight) marks the focus (R-UI-014).

docs.title: Scaling
docs.text: scale: fit scales the design space by one factor, keeps the aspect ratio, centres it and fills the rest with outside; integer uses the largest whole multiple that fits; stretch (the testbed layout's) fills the window, x and y separately. filter: nearest keeps pixel art sharp. Text is drawn at the window's resolution. A screen may list aspects alternatives, and a remaster may replace a screen with one in a wider design space (R-UI-015).

docs.title: Two layouts
docs.text:
The screen set is the default where a campaign defines one; the testbed layout is the single-grid strategy screen of app 0.16, kept for testing and as the fallback. The player switches in Options (remembered per campaign as interface.layout in settings.yaml). The testbed layout's placement moves to its own key; an old screens.starmap whose widgets are all plain rectangles naming testbed widgets is still read as it, with a --check warning (R-UI-018).

testbed_layout:               # was screens.starmap in app 0.16.0 – 0.16.14
  design: [1280, 720]
  widgets: {top: [0, 0, 1280, 44], map: [8, 52, 790, 660], nav: [806, 52, 466, 72],
            info: [806, 132, 466, 212], panel: [806, 352, 466, 360]}

docs.title: Worked example: the CSD and the Orders dialog
docs.text:
The shape of interceptor's CSD and its Orders dialog. The coordinates and resource ids below are illustrative placeholders, not the mapped values: the real ones come from the mapping of WrappersDLL.dll, each marked verified or derived in the pack (R-UI-020). No art is copied — every image is a reference into the player's own file.

# packs/interceptor/interface/screens.yaml (illustrative)
campaign:
  interface: {layout: screens, home: starmap, scale: fit, filter: nearest}

screens:
  starmap:                                   # the CSD
    design: [640, 480]
    background: original:WrappersDLL.dll#<csd>
    clock: runs
    widgets:
      map:      {type: map, rect: [8, 8, 464, 464], shape: round, hover: hover_box}
      hover_box: {type: text, rect: [480, 8, 152, 60], bind: selected.summary, font: small}  # object, class, owner
      minimap:  {type: minimap, rect: [480, 76, 152, 96], map: map}
      globe:    {type: globe, rect: [480, 180, 152, 120], animation: original:WrappersDLL.dll#<globe>}
      lamp_contact: {type: lamp, rect: [500, 196, 12, 12], bind: alert.contact,
                     images: {off: original:WrappersDLL.dll#<lamps>@[0, 0, 12, 12],
                              on:  original:WrappersDLL.dll#<lamps>@[12, 0, 12, 12]}}
      clock:    {type: clock, rect: [480, 308, 152, 16], show: [time]}
      date:     {type: value, rect: [480, 326, 74, 14], bind: date, align: left}
      money:    {type: value, rect: [558, 326, 74, 14], bind: money, format: "@orig.<money_format>", align: right}
      to_bases: {type: button, rect: [480, 348, 74, 28], action: "open(bases)", key: B,
                 images: {up:   original:WrappersDLL.dll#<csd>@[480, 348, 74, 28],
                          down: original:WrappersDLL.dll#<csd_down>@[480, 348, 74, 28]}}
      # … five more screen buttons: research, purchase, pilots, reports, encyclopaedia
      speed_1:  {type: toggle, rect: [480, 452, 24, 20], group: speed, value: 1, default: true}
      # … the other speeds

  orders:                                    # the Interceptor Orders dialog, over the CSD
    dialog: true
    rect: [120, 140, 400, 200]
    frame: original:WrappersDLL.dll#<orders>
    dim: 0.4
    widgets:
      ships:    {type: list, rect: [132, 160, 376, 90], source: ships, row_height: 12,
                 columns: [{bind: name, width: 140}, {bind: pilot, width: 120}, {bind: status, width: 116}]}
      attack:   {type: button, rect: [132, 260, 180, 20], text: "@orig.<attack>", action: [attack, close]}
      redirect: {type: button, rect: [328, 260, 180, 20], text: "@orig.<new_destination>", action: [set_destination, close]}
      home:     {type: button, rect: [132, 290, 180, 20], text: "@orig.<return>", action: [return_to_base, close]}
      home_5s:  {type: button, rect: [328, 290, 180, 20], text: "@orig.<return_5s>", action: [return_to_base, close, run_for(5s)]}

The default campaign writes the same screens in its own design space with its generated art-deco images (images/ui/…, made by tools/default_assets), and any screen it leaves out opens the built-in version (R-UI-022).

docs.title: Cockpits and HUD
docs.text:
Cockpits stay as implemented (cockpits): 2D art at any resolution, its own design space, or a 3D model; instrument rectangles, or instruments anchored on the 3D model's surface. Additions:

  • instruments: {comms: …}: the MFD talking-head panel (the original's 113 Smacker clips; any image sequence or video for mods). As built (app 0.13.1): not a cockpit instrument but a fixed panel at the top left, driven by the voice sets — name and face (a picture or a looping Smacker clip, also original:mfdanim.mps#<member>) — and chatter's speaker (Radio voices › Faces). Custom instruments are not built.
  • custom instruments (instruments: {<custom>: …}) bound to a query (hull, plan(eclipse)) with a gauge style — for campaign-specific instruments.
  • Per-environment HUD elements (altitude and vertical speed, horizon line) shown only in atmospheric battles.

docs.title: Text: text/<language>/*.yaml
docs.text:
# text/en/ships.yaml
text:
  ship.lightning.name: X-1A Lightning II
  ship.lightning.desc: …
  msg.alien_2: "An intercepted transmission speaks of a fleet massing near {system}."
  • Every player-visible string is a text key (name: "@ship.lightning.name" in rules). Missing keys show the key itself and are reported by --check.
  • {variables} are filled from the context ({system}, {corporation}, {pilot}, {money}, {date}), matching the original's [SYSTEMNAME]-style tokens.
  • Name pools (names: {star_names: [..], pilots.male_first: [..]}) and news items (news: {<id>: …} with headline, text and the event that publishes it) live here too.
  • The interceptor mod reads the original text by reference — text: original:LangFile1.txt imports its 3,782 keys under orig.* (format KEY "text" with ~ breaks), plus starcorp1.txt, Names1.txt, news1.txt, short1.txt — so no original text is copied into the mod.

docs.title: Encyclopaedia: encyclopaedias: {<id>: …}, entries: {<id>: …}
docs.text: Categories, entries with text keys, a model or image, stats pulled from the rules (stats: auto), and an unlock condition (unlocked: "research(x) or encountered(class)"). The original's nine categories and about 150 DATABANK_* entries map one-to-one.

docs.title: Music: music: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
The original uses interactive music: three sets, each with cruise, threat and battle states of five segments, plus death, victory and good/bad-result stingers, with transition tables (Loops/*.wtl). The format:

music:
  interceptor_set_1:
    states:
      cruise: [original:Loops/cruise1a.wav, original:Loops/cruise1b.wav]   # … five segments
      threat: […]
      battle: […]
    stingers: {death: …, victory: …}
    switch:
      - {to: threat, when: "enemies_detected"}
      - {to: battle, when: "enemies_within(5km)"}
      - {to: cruise}                  # otherwise
    transition: segment_end

Strategy-screen music, CD audio tracks (the original's Red Book audio, played from the player's ripped files) and the default campaign's synthesised loops use the same section.

As built (app 0.11.0)

states (cruise, threat, battle, strategy), stingers, and in place of switch: and transition: two ranges, threat_range and battle_range, with the transition always at a segment's end; plus volume. The interceptor files are named without the Loops/ folder (original:cruise1-1.wav; the original-data index finds them by name). Not built: switch: conditions, the .wtl tables, CD audio. Modding › Music, DEV-053.

docs.title: Voices and chatter
docs.text: voices: {<id>: …}: a set of lines for wingman and pilot chatter (the original's 5 male and 5 female voices × 60 lines, computer voice, alien and station lines), each line a text key plus an audio file. Missions trigger lines by event (chatter keys); pilots are assigned voices.

docs.title: Video
docs.text:
videos: {<id>: …}: intro, endings, cut-scenes. Smacker (the original; in-crate decoder, Stage 5) or an image sequence with audio for mods. An ending, briefing or chapter card may name a video.

As built (app 0.12.0 – 0.13.0)

No videos: section: a video is named directly by its asset reference — the story action video(<ref>), endings.<id>.video and campaign.intro_video — and only Smacker plays. Image sequences are not built (MD3).

Cutscenes played by the engine, and video files in place of them (through the operating system's media framework, with image sequences as the fallback), are designed on Mod designer, cutscene designer and game bundling (R-MOD-033 – R-MOD-046, planned).

docs.title: Revision history
docs.text: Version Date Change 1.0.0 2026-11-11 Adopted into Specification 1.0.0 as a normative format page; requirements link here 1.7.0 2026-11-11 Video: link to the cutscene and video-cutscene design 1.16.0 2026-11-11 As-built notes (app 0.11.0 – 0.13.1): skins, the comms panel, music, video 1.19.0 2026-11-12 The original-style multi-screen interface (user request; planned, plan item 6.9): the Screens table splits factory from market and adds options and the dialogs; new section Screen sets — campaign interface keys, screen keys, the widget catalogue, actions, bound values and lists, dialogs, focus and keys, scaling, the two layouts (testbed_layout), and a worked example of the CSD and the Orders dialog; an As-built note on the testbed layout (app 0.16.0). Requirements R-UI-001 – R-UI-040

docs.title: Format: missions, environments and events
docs.text:
Status: design; implemented in Stage 3 (missions, environments), Stage 4 (generation from the strategy layer) and Stage 5 (campaign events). Stage 3 part 1 (app 0.3.0) implemented mission types: roles, arrivals (as a role's at: / arrive:), waves, objectives, optional objectives, timer, outcomes as checked actions, chatter and debriefs, flown from the launcher — documented for modders on Missions. Hazards followed in app 0.5.1, environments, atmospheric flight, terrain and the atmosphere HUD in 0.6.0 and ground installations in 0.6.1 — documented on Missions › Hazards and Environments and terrain; the notes below mark what was built and how it differs from this design. Still planned: location, backdrop from the map, generated, refuse, roles from: the strategy situation, chatter voices, simulator missions, terrain detail textures and scattered objects, events and squadrons. Files in missions/*.yaml and events/*.yaml (YAML, like every mod file). The scenario format stays for testbed arenas; a mission is a scenario with roles, waves, objectives and outcomes.

In the original, mission composition is entirely hard-coded (27 briefing types, 7 side missions, 12 simulator types). The interceptor mod writes each one as a mission type below.

docs.title: Mission types: missions: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
missions:
  defend_outpost:
    name: "@mission.defend_outpost"
    briefing: "@brief.defend_outpost"            # text with {variables}
    location: outpost                            # location kind on the map
    environment: orbit                           # battle environment (below)
    backdrop: location                           # star, planet, belt of the map location
    generated: "squadron_targets(alien, outpost)"   # when the strategy layer creates it
    refuse: {score: refused_outpost_defence, relation: {owner: -6}}
    # Forces: roles filled from the strategy situation, with fallbacks for the testbed
    roles:
      station: {from: target_outpost, behaviour: station_guns}
      guards: {class: corporate_fighter, count: [2, 4], faction: owner, behaviour: corporate_guard}
      attackers: {from: attacking_squadron}
      player: {from: launched_craft}             # at most the campaign's max_craft_per_mission
    arrivals:
      attackers: {distance: 6km, from_role: station, time: 0s}
    waves:
      - {role: attackers, from: squadron_reserve, when: "time > 120s and alive(station)", at: random_edge}
    # Objectives
    objectives:
      win: "destroyed_all(attackers) or retreated_all(attackers)"
      lose: "destroyed(station)"
    optional:
      capture: "captured_any(attackers)"
    outcomes:
      win: [score(outpost_defended), salvage, "relation(owner, +8)"]
      lose: [lose(outpost), score(outpost_lost)]
      retreat: [score(refused_outpost_defence)]  # hyperspace out
    debrief: "@debrief.defend_outpost.{result}"
Key Meaning location, environment, backdrop Where the battle happens and what the arena is like. environment: <id> implemented (app 0.6.0; missions and scenarios); location and backdrop: location need the strategy map (Stage 4) — a planet backdrop is part of the environment for now. generated The strategy-layer condition that creates the mission (squadron meets asset, request, event). Testbed and story missions omit it. roles: {<name>: …} A group of objects: from the situation (the squadron that triggered it, the station under attack), from a class list with counts (per difficulty), or the player's launched craft. Each role has a behaviour and a faction. Implemented for class lists and counts (the player's craft is player:); from: the situation is Stage 4. arrivals: {<role>: …}, waves: [..] When and where groups enter: time, condition, position (distance and bearing, edge, near another role, hyperspace in). Implemented differently: arrival is part of each role — at: {distance, bearing, from, spread} and arrive: <condition> — not a separate arrivals: map (DEV-040). Waves implemented ({role, when, count, at}, each once). Edge and hyperspace-in arrivals: planned. objectives: {win, lose, draw}, optional: {<id>: …} Conditions; checked every tick. draw for draws (the original has win/draw/lose debriefs). Implemented (lose before win; optional objectives latched). outcomes: {<result>: [..]} Action lists: score, salvage, capture, relation changes, map changes (outpost lost), flags, story steps. Implemented as checked actions; message runs in battle, campaign actions are listed on the debrief until Stage 4 applies them. timer timer: {after: 10min, then: lose} for timed missions (the hijacked Nova Bomb, the arms dealer). Implemented. hazards Implemented (app 0.5.1; missions and scenarios), with explicit keys instead of the sketched shorthand: {asteroids: {class, count, radius, center, spin}, minefield: {class, count, radius, center, faction}, black_hole: {position, pull, radius}, ion_storm: {sensors: 40%}} — sensors is the fraction of radar range kept, not a reduction (R-MSN-009). chatter Radio lines by trigger. Implemented as - {when: <condition>, line: "@chat.more_bogeys"} (each said once); voices are planned. debrief Debrief text per result. Implemented.

Logistics missions (planned). convoy_ambush (an enemy attacks a supply convoy; destroyed or captured cargo never arrives) and construction_defence (an enemy strikes a facility before it is finished, from 50 % construction and at most three times per location; the facility appears in its construction-stage model) are generated by the strategy layer's logistics; a supply convoy's attack point is chosen at random at its launch (the 25 % attack roll belongs to survey ships); see Logistics.

Simulator missions (the original's combat simulator) are mission types with simulator: true and parameters chosen in a setup screen (params: {fighters: [1, 12], tech: [1, 3]}), with no campaign effects.

docs.title: Battle environments: environments: {<id>: …}
docs.text:
The original fights only in space: deep space, around stations, in asteroid belts and next to a black hole. The format also supports atmospheric and ground battles — attacks on and defence of surface installations such as mining colonies and research outposts. The default campaign uses them; the interceptor campaign does not.

As built (app 0.6.0 – 0.6.1)

Built: physics: space | atmosphere, arena, gravity, air_density, ceiling, terrain (the design's ground), an inline sky: {top, horizon, fog, fog_distance, stars} (the design names a sky), backdrop: {planet: {color, size, direction}}; terrains with generate: {kind: craters | hills, seed} or heightmap, a single size (square), height: [low, high] as plain metres, colors: {low, high, slope} and resolution. Open space is simply no environment: (there is no space entry to define). Not built: inherit between environments (the rules' own inherit works), speed_of_sound, weather, the terrain's texture (base and detail maps) and objects (scattered rocks). Reference: Environments and terrain.

environments:
  space:
    physics: space                      # newtonian: no drag, no gravity (the implemented model)
    arena: 60km                         # sphere radius
    backdrop: [starfield, location_bodies]
  orbit:
    inherit: space
    backdrop: [starfield, {planet: location, distance: 20000km}]
  atmosphere_rocky:
    physics: atmosphere
    gravity: 9.0                        # m/s², downwards (−Y)
    air_density: 1.0                    # scales drag and lift; 0 = vacuum (a moon)
    speed_of_sound: 330                 # optional: buffeting near it
    ground: rocky_moon                  # heightfield (below)
    ceiling: 12km                       # leaving the top = escaping to orbit (retreat)
    sky: dusk_violet                    # gradient, sun, clouds, fog distance
    weather: {dust: 0.3}                # visibility and sensor range factor

terrains:
  rocky_moon:
    heightmap: textures/terrain/rocky_hm.png     # or generate: {kind: craters, seed: 7}
    size: [40km, 40km]
    height: [0m, 2500m]
    texture: {base: textures/terrain/rocky.png, detail: textures/terrain/rock_detail.png}
    objects: {scatter: "models/rock_*.obj", density: 0.002}

docs.title: Atmospheric flight
docs.text:
When physics: atmosphere, the flight model adds forces the space model does not have, so the same ship flies very differently on a planet:
